Changing it re-arms. frame | second | minute | hour | day | number

entries.title: Time.running
entries.text: The live gate — running = { app.simulating } is the idiom; default true. The first frame after a start is the baseline and reports no step. boolean

entries.title: Time.now
entries.text: The instant, epoch milliseconds — per frame at tick = frame, at the flip otherwise. number

entries.title: Time.year
entries.text: The local-zone year. number

entries.title: Time.month
entries.text: The local-zone month, 1–12. number

entries.title: Time.day
entries.text: The day of the month, 1–31. number

entries.title: Time.hour
entries.text: The local-zone hour, 0–23. number

entries.title: Time.minute
entries.text: 0–59. number

entries.title: Time.second
entries.text: 0–59. number

entries.title: Time.weekday
entries.text: 1–7, Monday = 1 (ISO, as Temporal). number

entries.title: Time.tick
entries.text: onTick(dt) — one call per tick while running, with the seconds elapsed since the previous tick, clamped to about one tick (≈1/15 s at frame; one period on the calendar tiers, so a page returning from an hour hidden gets 60, not 3600). Three consecutive throws stop the Time, loudly, naming the node; running = true restarts it. A clock is not a way to hear about a change. A Time gated on a condition, whose handler does its work and closes its own gate, is asking to be told that something crossed into a new state. Name the value in trackChanges and answer onChange (Node): it runs at the close of the settle that moved the value, not on the next frame, and it costs no clock. onTick(e: number)

entries.title: Keys
entries.text: The keyboard, as a member. Keys names one concept that a program can either ask or listen to: Keys.isDown("KeyA") is a call you make from any { } body; a Keys [ … ] member is how the keyboard calls you. It is the raw stream — it fires even while a text field has focus, so gate app-level shortcuts on app state where that matters. A focused view's own onKeyDown/onKeyUp handlers are the other half of the story, and usually the right one for keys that belong to a particular widget. Lifetime is the node's: subscribed at init, dropped when the node is discarded, nothing to clean up. Fan-out is by instance — a menu, a dialog, and a menubar each holding a Keys member all hear the keyboard at once. App [ width = 240, height = 100, fill = white, textColor = black, n: number = 0, keys: Keys [ onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent) { if (e.key == "ArrowUp") { app.n = app.n + 1 } else if (e.key == "ArrowDown") { app.n = app.n - 1 } } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 30, fontSize = 30, text = { n = ${n} } ] ]

entries.title: Keys.isDown
entries.text: Whether a key is physically down right now, by code ("ShiftLeft", "MetaLeft") — for modifier state at the moment of a gesture, which is not carried on a pointer event. How a table decides whether a click extends a range or toggles one member. onClick() { (parent as Table).rowClick(this.rowIndex(), this.member(), Keys.isDown("MetaLeft") Keys.isDown("ControlLeft"), Keys.isDown("ShiftLeft")) } isDown(code: string): boolean

entries.title: Keys.held
entries.text: Every key currently down, as code strings. held(): string[]

entries.title: Keys.navClaim
entries.text: Claims the navigation keys — arrows, Space, Home/End, Page — away from the browser's scroll defaults while an overlay is roving, and releases them when passed false. An open menu owns the arrow keys ; without the claim the page scrolls underneath it. Claim on open, release on close, always in pairs — a claim that outlives its overlay leaves the page unscrollable. navClaim(owner: object, on: boolean): void

entries.title: Keys.keyDown
entries.text: onKeyDown(e) — a key went down. e is a normalized KeyEvent: e.key ("ArrowUp", "Escape", "a"), e.code, and modifier flags — never a numeric code. onKeyDown(e: KeyEvent)

entries.title: Keys.keyUp
entries.text: onKeyUp(e) — a key came up, same payload. onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent)

entries.title: Keys.navClaim
entries.text: The navigation keys changed hands: true when something claimed them (an overlay opened and its arrows now rove it), false when the last claim released. It fires on the transition only, not per claim, so nested overlays that each claim do not chatter. This is how a focus ring stands down while a menu owns the arrows: the library's own ring subscribes to it, because during that time the menu's rover is the focus and a second indicator would be a lie. onNavClaim(e: boolean)

entries.title: Focus
entries.text: The focus service, as a member. Like Keys, Focus names one concept a program can ask (Focus.focus(this), Focus.byKeyboard() — calls from any { } body) or listen to (a Focus [ … ] member). Listening is what a focus indicator does: the library's FocusRing follows focus with exactly these two handlers, tracking where focus went and the live silhouette of whatever holds it. Most apps never need it — focus rings, tab order, and activation are provided — but replacing the indicator is a supported thing to do, and this is how. watch: Focus [ onFocusChange(v: View) { classroot.target = v }, onGeometry(g: FocusGeometry) { classroot.tx = g.x; classroot.ty = g.y } ]

entries.title: Focus.focus
entries.text: Moves keyboard focus to a view — the only way to move it; assigning a control's focused does not. The call every control makes on pointer-down, so that the keyboard picks up where the pointer left off. Focusing a view that is not focusable is a no-op. onPointerDown() { Focus.focus(this) } focus(v: unknown): void

entries.title: Focus.blur
entries.text: Clears focus entirely, so nothing holds it. blur(): void

entries.title: Focus.next
entries.text: Moves focus to the next view in traversal order — what Tab does, callable directly when a control wants to advance focus itself (a field that moves on Enter). next(): void

entries.title: Focus.prev
entries.text: Moves focus to the previous view in traversal order — Shift-Tab's action. prev(): void

entries.title: Focus.byKeyboard
entries.text: Whether the current focus arrived by keyboard rather than by pointer — the web's :focus-visible rule, as a reactive read. This is what lets a clicked control show no focus edge while a tabbed one does, and what a focus indicator keys off to decide whether to appear at all. byKeyboard(): boolean

entries.title: Focus.getFocus
entries.text: The view that currently holds focus, or null — for saving focus before opening a modal and restoring it after. Restore on a later turn, not immediately: an in-flight keystroke must finish against the old focus, or the key that closed a dialog is delivered to the opener, which reopens it. getFocus(): any

entries.title: Focus.focusChange
entries.text: onFocusChange(v) — focus moved to view v (or null when nothing is focused). onFocusChange(v: View)

entries.title: Focus.geometry
entries.text: onGeometry(g) — the focused control's live root-space silhouette: g.x, g.y, g.w, g.h, g.rad (its corner radius), g.view, and g.root (the app that owns it — an embedded app's ring ignores a target belonging to another). onGeometry(g: FocusGeometry)

entries.title: Tip
entries.text: The tooltip service, as a member: onTip(e) fires when a view carrying tip = "…" wants its tooltip shown, and with null when it should hide. The service owns the platform conventions — the show delay, instant retarget while showing, hide on press — so a listener only renders. The library's Tooltip is the one listener most programs ever need, and it arrives automatically in any app whose views carry tips. Declare your own Tip [ … ] member only when you are replacing that rendition. tips: Tip [ onTip(e: TipEvent) { if (e == null) { classroot.shown = false; return } classroot.label = e.text classroot.shown = true } ]

entries.title: Tip.tip
entries.text: onTip(e) — show the tip described by e (e.text, plus the target's root-space box e.x/e.y/e.w/e.h and its owning app e.root), or hide when e is null. onTip(e: TipEvent)

entries.title: Stream
entries.text: The abstract base of the live-connection sources — EventStream (SSE) and Socket (WebSocket) extend it. Not instantiable: write the concrete transport. The one thing to know: there is no connect() or disconnect() — the declaration decides. A stream is connected exactly while active is true and url is non-empty; empty the url (or flip active) and it closes, change the url and it closes and reopens, remove the node and the connection dies with it. Nothing to unsubscribe, ever. Messages are transient: nothing accumulates unless a handler writes it somewhere — the runtime keeps only last. An app that streams JSON parses in the handler (JSON.parse(e.data)) and writes wherever it wants; accumulation is one line of app code, deliberately not a built-in policy. chat: View [ answer: string = "", reply: EventStream [ url = { /api/chat?id=${classroot.chatId} }, active = { classroot.chatId != "" }, onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { classroot.answer = classroot.answer + e.data }, ], out: Text [ width = { parent.width }, text = { parent.answer } ] ]

entries.title: Stream.url
entries.text: Where to connect — a literal or a { } constraint. Unlike DataSource.url, a change acts immediately: the old connection closes and a new one opens at the new address (there is no fetch() moment to wait for). "" means detached — the idiom for "no conversation yet" is deriving emptiness: url = { app.chatId != "" ? "/api/chat/" + app.chatId : "" }. string

entries.title: Stream.active
entries.text: The gate. false closes the connection (and cancels any pending retry); flipping back true reopens it. Constrain it to app state — active = { app.live } — rather than toggling imperatively. boolean

entries.title: Stream.retry
entries.text: Reconnect policy, visible in the declaration: seconds to wait before re-dialing after the connection is lost and the platform won't bring it back on its own — a Socket's unexpected close, an EventStream's terminal failure. 0 (the default) means no retry: the stream lands in status = "failed" and the app decides. A declared retry keeps trying while active is true, at a fixed interval — no invisible backoff, no give-up count. A structural failure (the factory itself refuses — headless extraction, a missing host service) never loops, whatever retry says. number

entries.title: Stream.status
entries.text: The connection lifecycle as one fact: "closed", "connecting", "open", "retrying", or "failed" (down, and will not reconnect). Read-only — computed for you; assigning it is a compile error. "retrying" covers both the platform's own recovery (SSE) and a declared retry waiting to re-dial. closed | connecting | open | retrying | failed

entries.title: Stream.error
entries.text: The last failure reason, "" when none; cleared when a connection opens. Read-only — the state side of onError (the event side). A status line is text = { feed.error != "" ? feed.error : feed.status }. string

entries.title: Stream.last
entries.text: The most recent message's data, reactive. Read-only. The zero-handler tier: a ticker that only shows the latest value needs no handler at all — text = { feed.last }. string

entries.title: Stream.open
entries.text: The boolean view of status == "open" — one fact, two spellings, never in disagreement. Read-only. The connection dot is visible = { feed.open }. boolean

entries.title: Stream.message
entries.text: onMessage(e: StreamMessage) — every message. e.data is always a string: parse it yourself if it is JSON, concatenate it if it is streamed text; the runtime never guesses. e.type is the SSE named event ("message" for unnamed messages and every socket frame); e.id is the SSE last-event-id ("" on sockets). onMessage(e: StreamMessage)

entries.title: Stream.open
entries.text: The connection is live — fires each time one opens, including reopens after a retry. Prefer deriving from open/status for anything a constraint can express; the handler is for work state cannot do (send a subscription frame, log). onOpen()

entries.title: Stream.close
entries.text: A connection that had opened went away — the app closed it (active, a url change, node removal at discard is silent), the server ended it, or it failed. Fires once per connection, before any retry dials the next one. onClose()

entries.title: Stream.error
entries.text: Something failed: a terminal connection loss, a refused transport, a send on a socket that is not open. The reason is in error when the handler runs. The platform's own in-flight retries (SSE) are not errors and stay quiet. onError()

entries.title: EventStream
entries.text: Server-Sent Events (text/event-stream) as a source — the streaming-AI shape: the server pushes, the app receives, an onMessage that concatenates is the whole consumer. See Stream for the shared surface (url/active/retry, the read-only status/open/error/last). Receive-only — there is no send; a request that needs a body is an ordinary DataSource POST, and the stream carries the reply. The platform's EventSource machinery is kept verbatim: it retries on its own (honoring the server's retry: hint) and resumes with Last-Event-ID, during which status reads "retrying" and no error is reported; retry/onError concern only terminal failure — the platform giving up. A declared stream holds a live connection for as long as it is active and its node lives — every open tab is one held server connection (browsers cap ~6 per host over HTTP/1.1, so a dev server's tabs can exhaust the pool). The lifecycle is the declaration: active = { app.chatId != "" } releases the connection the moment the condition goes false, and a discarded node closes its own — there is nothing to unsubscribe. answer: string = "", reply: EventStream [ url = { /api/chat?id=${app.chatId} }, active = { app.chatId != "" }, onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { app.answer = app.answer + e.data }, ]

entries.title: EventStream.listenTo
entries.text: The named SSE event types to deliver — listenTo = ["contentblockdelta", "message_stop"]. Required for any stream that labels messages with event: lines (Anthropic-style AI streams do): the platform's EventSource physically cannot deliver a named event it was not asked to listen for, so an undeclared name is silently invisible — if onMessage sees nothing but the connection is open, this is the first thing to check. The name carries the contract: you hear what you listen to. Unnamed (default) messages always arrive; e.type says which kind each one is. array

entries.title: Socket
entries.text: WebSocket as a source: the Stream surface plus send(text) — send is a call you make, onMessage is it calling you. See Stream for url/active/retry and the read-only status/open/error/last. Unlike SSE the platform has no native reconnect, so a Socket that should survive a dropped connection must say so: retry = 2 re-dials two seconds after any close the app didn't ask for, for as long as active holds — the whole policy is that one number. Text frames only; a binary frame is dropped. live: Socket [ url = "wss://api.example.com/feed", retry = 2, onOpen() { this.send('{"subscribe":"prices"}') }, onMessage(e: StreamMessage) { app.tick(JSON.parse(e.data)) }, ]

entries.title: Socket.send
entries.text: Sends one text frame. Legal only while open — on a socket that is not open it sends nothing and reports through the error channel (error + onError), never a silent queue: if the app needs buffering-until-connected, that policy belongs in app state, visibly. Sending the opening frame belongs in onOpen (which also covers every reconnect); gate user-triggered sends on .open. send(text: string): void

entries.title: State
entries.text: A named bundle of overrides that snaps on and off together. Its body is not ordinary children: a name = value entry is an override of the enclosing view's own attribute (checked against that view's schema, not the State's), applied while the state is on; an id: Type [ … ] entry is a conditional subtree that exists only while applied. Because attribute reads compose as a precedence stack, the base values return exactly when the state turns off — there is no manual undo to write, and no drift. card: View [ height = 72, fill = white, open: State [ applied = { expanded }, height = 184, fill = lightsteelblue, Text [ text = "shown only while open" ] ] ]

entries.title: State.applied
entries.text: Whether the state is on. Constrain it to a condition (applied = { expanded }) and the whole bundle snaps in and out as that flips — the base values restore themselves when it turns off. The declarative alternative to the apply() / remove() / toggle() verbs. boolean

entries.title: State.apply
entries.text: Turns the bundle on imperatively — the verb form of applied = true. Prefer constraining applied to a condition; reach for apply() only when the toggle is truly event-driven and has no natural boolean to constrain it to. apply(): void

entries.title: State.remove
entries.text: Turns the bundle off, restoring the base values via the precedence stack (no manual undo). The partner of apply(). remove(): void

entries.title: State.toggle
entries.text: Flips the bundle on/off from its current state — a one-call switch for a handler (onClick() { panel.toggle() }) when you don't want to thread a boolean. toggle(): void

entries.title: State.apply
entries.text: Fires when the bundle turns on — after the overrides compose onto the stack, so reads in the handler already see the state's values. Use for a side effect that must ride with the state (focus a revealed field), not to mutate what the state already declares. onApply()

entries.title: State.remove
entries.text: Fires when the bundle turns off, the partner of onApply — after the base values have restored. For tearing down whatever onApply set up. onRemove()

entries.title: Node
entries.text: The plain object-graph atom — a non-visual node you subclass for logic that isn't a view: a controller, a coordinator, a service. A bare class X [ … ] defaults its base to Node, so a class with attributes and methods but no box is a Node subclass. It lives in the tree as a named member, shares the reactive core and the classroot/app reach, and fires init — but it paints nothing. Reach for it instead of a View when a wrapper class would be visual in name only. class Cart [ count: number = 0, add() { count = count + 1 }, clear() { count = 0 } ] A view then holds one as a named member (cart: Cart [ ]) and reads/drives it reactively — state and behaviour with no pixels of its own. A Node may also stand on a record with a datapath of its own: its :path reads and :field = v writes resolve against that record, so a model class owns the rules for a kind of data with no view involved. A class meant to be a box needs extends View — class Box [ width = 40 ] is refused ("Box has no attribute 'width'").

entries.title: Node.trackChanges
entries.text: The values this node reports changes to: trackChanges = [ "loaded", "kind" ]. Each name must be one of the node's own reactive values — an attribute it declares, a fact it carries (scrollY, loaded, hot), or an attribute bound to data. The checker refuses a stranger in a written list, and the runtime refuses one in a computed list when the node arms. To hear a record's field, declare an attribute over the path (kind: string = { :kind }) and name that — there is one door. Nothing else is tracked, so a node that names nothing costs nothing. array

entries.title: Node.datapath
entries.text: The data cursor: the place in a dataset this node and its descendants read and write relative to. Written as a :path (extending the inherited cursor), a { } expression yielding a place (datapath = { app.d.value.tasks[app.pick] }), or null. The nearest ancestor-or-self cursor wins, so a model class with its own datapath stands on that record, and views inside it read the same one. A :path ending in [] replicates — and only a view replicates; on any other node that form is a compile error naming the single-record spelling. datapath

entries.title: Node.$data
entries.text: Reads the datum at a path relative to the nearest cursor — this node's own, or the nearest ancestor's — the compiled form every :path lowers to, callable by hand. $data("") is the whole record at the cursor, which is what a replicated row calls to hand its own record to a method. Reach for the :path spelling in ordinary code; reach for this when the path is computed, or when you need the record itself rather than a field of it. member() -> object { return this.datapath != null ? this.$data("") : this } $data(path: string | readonly unknown[]): unknown

entries.title: Node.$cell
entries.text: The compiled form of a write to a record field: a handler's :done = v lowers to this.$cell(["done"]).value = v, and :n += 1 reads and writes through the same place. The write lands through the dataset's set, relative to the nearest cursor, exactly where the matching read resolves. Write :field = v; this is what the compiler emits, not a call to make by hand. $cell(segs: readonly unknown[]): { value: unknown }

entries.title: Node.init
entries.text: Fires once when the node has finished constructing and its subtree exists — the place for setup that needs the built tree. Every node gets it, faceless subclasses included — the init walk visits non-View children too. Answered by onInit(). onInit()

entries.title: Node.change
entries.text: Fires at the close of a settle in which one or more tracked values ended different from where they started: after every constraint has re-run and every reader already holds the new value. One call per settle carries all of them, so a node whose two subjects move together acts once. Answered by onChange(e: ChangeEvent), where e.changed holds one ValueChange per value — its name, its previousValue (what it held at the previous close), and its currentValue (what the node holds now; reading the attribute directly gives the same thing). Silent at boot: first values are not changes, and setup belongs in onInit or, for the whole tree, the App's onReady. A handler's writes are the next settle, so a change may cause a change; a handler may not assign a value it was told about, and a ring of handlers ends on its own, because a value is delivered at most once per settle chain. Not to be confused with an input's edits, which is the instinct the name carries in from HTML and React: a field reports what the reader typed through onInput, and a control reports its own value through input(). This event is about a value the program holds. Use it only for a genuine state change — something happened and the program must act once: mark a conversation read when the reader reaches its end, open a pane when the data lands, start a fetch when a selection changes. It is not for following a value, which is a constraint, nor for moving one, which is a Spring, and it is not meant for use in conjunction with animation. onChange(e: ChangeEvent)

entries.title: Bar
entries.text: A labeled horizontal value bar: an optional caption, then a rounded track filled to value, in a colour you choose. It is for demos and dashboards that want a caption and their own colour; for a meter that follows the theme, use ProgressBar. col: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ], Bar [ width = 260, label = "Storage", value = 72 ], Bar [ width = 260, label = "Memory", value = 38, tint = #37E0C8 ] ]

entries.title: Bar.label
entries.text: The caption to the left of the track. "" drops the caption column entirely and the track takes the full width. string

entries.title: Bar.value
entries.text: How full the track reads, 0–100 always — a percentage, not your own units. This is the difference from ProgressBar, which takes min/max and lets you pass raw counts. number

entries.title: Bar.tint
entries.text: The fill colour. The one restyling knob — Bar carries literal colour defaults rather than theme tokens, so it does not follow a theme the way library controls do. Color

entries.title: Bar.lead
entries.text: The caption column's width, derived from whether there is a label at all. Set it to align several bars whose captions differ in length. number

entries.title: Bar.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Card
entries.text: The box everything else sits on: the theme's surface fill, its corner radius, a hairline edge in its line token, and — the part that saves the wrapper view — a default layout that stacks and pads, so a Card's children are written as a plain list and arrive inset from every edge. Card [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 280, Text [ fontSize = 15, fontWeight = semibold, text = "Storage" ], Text [ width = 100%, wrap = true, text = "Cards size themselves to what they hold, padding included." ], Divider [ ], Button [ label = "Manage" ] ] Use Text, not TextLabel, as a direct child. A TextLabel positions itself vertically — that cap-centering y is the whole of what it adds — and the card's layout places the children it holds, so the two would own the same slot. TextLabel belongs inside a control or a row that leaves y alone; a card's own lines are Text. Give it a width, not a height. A Card has no height of its own: it takes the one its content needs, padding counted in — so the box grows and shrinks with what is inside it, and nothing has to be kept in step by hand. Set height only to cap it (with clip = true if the content may exceed the cap). The inset is the card's own padding = 16, a View attribute: the card has an inside, and every child — stacked by the default layout, placing itself at x = center, or opted out with ignoreLayout — is positioned from it. The default arrangement is SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ], which simply stacks inside that room, 8 apart. Replacing the layout does not replace the padding. Naming your own layout: member — a WrappingLayout, a row, a stack with different numbers — overrides the arrangement only; the card is still inset, because the inset was never the arrangement's. Write padding = 0 to take it away, or padding = 24 for more. fill, cornerRadius and stroke are ordinary defaults a use site may write over the same way.

entries.title: Card.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record the card styles off. Reads surface for the fill, line for the edge, and controlRadius for the corners — the tokens every preset carries, so a card is the theme's surface in all four, light and dark. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: Card.fill
entries.text: The theme's surface — the token that means "the plane content sits on", one step off the window's own bg in every preset, light and dark. Write over it for a card that should sink into the page rather than rise off it (fill = { theme.bg }), and pair that with a kept stroke so the shape still reads. Fill

entries.title: Card.cornerRadius
entries.text: The theme's controlRadius, so a card's corners match the buttons and fields inside it — 7 in the house look, 4 in Redmond and MountainView. Set a number to break with the preset; the box still clips nothing unless you also say clip = true. Radius

entries.title: Card.stroke
entries.text: A one-pixel edge in the theme's line. stroke = null removes it — the right move for a card that already stands off the page by fill alone, or one nested inside another. Per-side works here as anywhere: stroke = [ null, null, stroke(1, #DBE1E9), null ] turns a card into a row with a rule under it. Stroke

entries.title: Card.padding
entries.text: Inset

entries.title: Divider
entries.text: A single line in the theme's line token, sized to the room it is given: drop one into a stack and it spans the content, drop one into a row with axis = y and it stands on end. It is a painted view, not a border — which is what lets it be a child in a list like any other, and lets a layout space it like any other. Card [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 280, Text [ text = "General" ], Divider [ ], Text [ text = "Advanced" ] ] thickness is logical pixels, not device pixels. 1 is one of the units everything else in a program is measured in, so on a 2× display the rule is two device pixels and looks like every other 1px edge in the library — there is no hairline primitive here.

entries.title: Divider.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record the rule takes its line colour from — set once by the app, read here by name. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: Divider.axis
entries.text: Which way the rule runs: x (the default) is horizontal and spans the parent's width; y is vertical and spans its height. A bare literal, not a string. The span is the parent's content extent — the room inside the parent's own padding — so a divider in a padded card stops where the card's content does, rather than running out under the inset. Axis

entries.title: Divider.thickness
entries.text: The rule's weight in logical pixels. 1 is the library's hairline everywhere. number

entries.title: Divider.inset
entries.text: How far in from the leading edge the rule starts — the list-separator convention, where a row's separator begins under the text rather than under the icon beside it. The rule's far end stays put, so the inset shortens it. 0 (the default) is a full-span rule. number

entries.title: Divider.color
entries.text: The rule's colour, the theme's line by default. Set it for a rule that must read heavier or lighter than the theme's edges — a section break against a row separator. Color

entries.title: Divider.width
entries.text: Derived, not authored: the span across the rule on a horizontal divider, thickness on a vertical one. Leave it alone — writing a width here fights the span, and a shorter rule is what inset is for. Length

entries.title: Divider.height
entries.text: The mirror of width: thickness on a horizontal rule, the span on a vertical one. Also derived, and also not for setting — a divider is as long as the room it was given. Length

entries.title: Divider.span
entries.text: span()

entries.title: Control
entries.text: The interaction-state base every stateful control extends. It owns how the pointer, keyboard, and focus relate to this view — and nothing semantic: checked, value, and their kin live on the concrete control. The pointer half is the language's: hovered and pressed are View's read-only interaction intrinsics (chain-based, touch-correct, cancel-safe). What Control adds is the control policy on top of them, as derivations every concrete control reads: hot / down — the styling pair: the intrinsics gated by disabled, with the keyboard-activation flash folded into down. Style against these, not the raw intrinsics, and a disabled control never lights up. disabled — inert: not focusable, no activation; concrete controls gate on it. keyboard — Space or Enter on the focused control activates it, the same press() path a pointer uses, acknowledged by flashing the pressed look. It also owns two things every labelled control shares: iconLeft / iconRight — decoration, by class name. A concrete control lays them out; Control only declares that they exist, so every control that shows one names it the same way. menu — the role of dropping a menu, not decoration. Setting menu gets the disclosure mark, the anchored open, the held-open styling, and ArrowDown-to-open together, which is the part a hand-rolled copy gets wrong one piece at a time. Extend it to make your own control a first-class one — focusable, keyboard-activated, and styled off the same state pair as everything the library ships: class Stepper extends Control [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, n: number = 0, fill = { down ? theme.controlPressed : hot ? theme.controlHover : theme.control }, press() { n = n + 1 }, onClick() { if (!disabled) press() }, t: TextLabel [ x = center, fontSize = 13, text = { "" + classroot.n } ] ] App [ Stepper [ x = 20, y = 20 ] ]

entries.title: Control.theme
entries.text: The design-token record every widget styles off — a provided value. An app provides it once (App [ theme = { app.dark ? SanFranciscoDark : SanFrancisco } ]) and Control reads it here, so a control body reads theme.accent as a plain, typed member. The default is SanFrancisco, so a control in an app that never mentions a theme still renders. Provide a different record on a subtree to reskin it; every provided("theme") below reads the nearer one. Theme

entries.title: Control.disabled
entries.text: Inert: not focusable, no activation, and the gate folded into hot/down so a disabled control never lights up. Constrain it rather than assigning it (disabled = { app.muted }) — it is ordinary derived state. Concrete controls also dim themselves against theme.disabledOpacity. boolean

entries.title: Control.focused
entries.text: True while this control holds keyboard focus. For the ring, you want nothing: the app-level FocusRing indicates focus for you. Read this only for a control's own focus styling. boolean

entries.title: Control.hot
entries.text: Hover under control policy — hovered gated by disabled. Style against this, not the raw hovered intrinsic , or a disabled control lights up under the pointer. Always false on touch, since hovered is. boolean

entries.title: Control.down
entries.text: The pressed look — the pressed intrinsic gated by disabled, with keyboard activation folded in , so Space/Enter flashes the same appearance a pointer press gives. The other half of the styling pair with hot. boolean

entries.title: Control.focusVisible
entries.text: Focused and the focus arrived by keyboard — the web's :focus-visible channel. Cleared by blur and by a pointer press on this control, so a clicked control shows no keyboard edge while a tabbed one does. What a Pane header's focus edge reads. boolean

entries.title: Control.iconLeft
entries.text: A decorative icon for the leading slot, named by class (iconLeft = "TrashIcon"), not nested as a child — a control is a leaf, and a name is the one form where authored and data-bound are the same mechanism (iconLeft = { "" + :icon } in a replicated toolbar). Control only declares the slot; the concrete control lays it out. A computed name needs use [ Name ] to survive the build, since no static reference reaches it. The name is read once, when the control is built: a name read from data gives each row its own icon, but changing the name later does not swap the icon (see IconHost). string

entries.title: Control.iconRight
entries.text: The trailing icon slot, same vocabulary as iconLeft. Setting it wins over the chevron a menu would imply — see rightIcon. string

entries.title: Control.menu
entries.text: The menu this control drops — an instance, not a name (menu = { app.optionsMenu }). Setting it is a role, not decoration: the disclosure mark, the anchored open below the control, the held-open fill, and ArrowDown-to-open all follow together. Declare one menu and point many controls at it rather than one per opener; the menu reads opener to vary its items. View

entries.title: Control.menuOpen
entries.text: True while menu is showing and this control is what opened it. Derived, never written — a flag set on open goes stale the moment the menu closes some other way (Escape, a pick, a press on the backdrop) and strands the control in its held-open look forever. boolean

entries.title: Control.rightIcon
entries.text: What actually renders on the right: iconRight when set, else the disclosure chevron implied by menu, else nothing. One place decides, so every menu-dropping control wears the same mark. string

entries.title: Control.flash
entries.text: The keyboard-activation pulse — the control's own state, since the pressed intrinsic is the pointer's truth and is read-only. Folded into down, so styling needs to read only the pair. boolean

entries.title: Control.flashMs
entries.text: How long flashPress() holds the pressed look. number

entries.title: Control.focusable
entries.text: A control takes focus unless it is disabled — one rule, so a disabled control drops out of the Tab order without saying so twice. boolean

entries.title: Control.openMenu
entries.text: Opens menu anchored to this control, unless there is none or the control is disabled. The seam a concrete control calls from its own press(). openMenu()

entries.title: Control.press
entries.text: The activation seam — override this, not the handlers. Pointer and keyboard both land here, so one override serves a click, Space, and Enter. The base opens menu when there is one. A value control delivers through input from here and never writes its own value slot directly , which is what lets a constrained control avoid fighting its constraint. press()

entries.title: Control.focusShape
entries.text: The focus silhouette the ring hugs, { x, y, w, h, rad } in this control's own coordinates. null (the default) rings the whole bounds at its cornerRadius. Override to ring the part that means something — a Radio rings its dot, a Slider its thumb. focusShape()

entries.title: Control.flashPress
entries.text: Flashes the pressed look to acknowledge keyboard activation — the platform convention for buttons and menu items. Value controls whose state change is itself the feedback (Checkbox, Switch, Radio) deliberately do not call it. flashPress()

entries.title: Control.focus
entries.text: Records focus and captures the keyboard modality into focusVisible. An override must keep both or the focus channel goes dark. onFocus()

entries.title: Control.blur
entries.text: Clears focused and focusVisible. onBlur()

entries.title: Control.pointerDown
entries.text: Claims focus, clears the :focus-visible channel, and opens menu if there is one — menus open on press, not release, as the platform does. An override must keep the Focus.focus(this) call , or clicking the control strands the keyboard elsewhere. onPointerDown()

entries.title: Control.keyDown
entries.text: Space and Enter run press(); ArrowDown opens menu. Ignores auto-repeat. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: Checkbox
entries.text: A boolean control. Its value is the checked attribute; input owns the value's destination — by default the destination is the checkbox itself, so it works standalone with zero wiring: mute: Checkbox [ label = "Mute" ] … visible = { mute.checked } Hand the value to its real owner by overriding input and constraining down: Checkbox [ label = "Mute", checked = { app.muted }, input(v: boolean) { app.muted = v } ] press() never writes checked directly — it only delivers — so a constrained checkbox never fights its constraint. row: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ], mute: Checkbox [ label = "Mute" ], Text [ text = { mute.checked ? "muted" : "audible" } ] ]

entries.title: Checkbox.baseline
entries.text: The baseline a row aligns this control by — the label's. Under align = baseline the checkbox's caption sits on the same line as its neighbours; the box rides with it. number

entries.title: Checkbox.checked
entries.text: Whether the box is ticked. Standalone it owns this and you read it back by name; constrained (checked = { app.muted }) it needs an input override to go with it — a constraint with no input leaves the checkbox's own edit assigning to a constrained slot, which is refused at runtime. boolean

entries.title: Checkbox.label
entries.text: The text beside the box. "" renders the box alone — the form for a checkbox inside a table cell, where the column heading is the label. string

entries.title: Checkbox.size
entries.text: The box's edge length. Defaults to the theme's figure, so a toolbar checkbox can shrink to match its neighbours without a subclass. number

entries.title: Checkbox.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Checkbox.width
entries.text: Content-sized: the box, then a gap and the label when there is one. A label-less checkbox is exactly its box, so a bare mark in a table cell reserves no phantom room. Length

entries.title: Checkbox.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole control — every part alike, never a recolour — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none: the one place the number lives. number

entries.title: Checkbox.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the box alone, not the box-plus-label — the Radio rule, so a long label does not drag a wide ring across the row. focusShape()

entries.title: Checkbox.input
entries.text: Where the value goes. The default writes checked; override it and the checkbox becomes a delivery channel for state you own (input(v: boolean) { app.muted = v }). This is the one member to override when the value lives elsewhere. input(v)

entries.title: Checkbox.press
entries.text: Toggles by delivering the flipped value through input — never by writing checked, which is what keeps a constrained checkbox from fighting its constraint. Called by a click and by Space/Enter. press()

entries.title: Checkbox.click
entries.text: Runs press() when enabled. Override input instead if what you want is the value. onClick()

entries.title: Button
entries.text: A labeled action control. The action is its onClick — write it at the use site exactly as on any View; Button adds the interaction states, the themed look, and keyboard activation (Space/Enter drives the same onClick). primary = true fills with the accent; the default is the quiet control look. Button [ label = "Save", primary = true ] Button [ label = "Add", iconLeft = "PlusIcon" ] Button [ label = "Options", menu = { app.optionsMenu } ] // chevron implied Button [ iconLeft = "CloseIcon" ] // icon only Three slots in a row — iconLeft, the label, iconRight — laid out by SimpleLayout and sized from contentWidth, so an absent label or icon costs nothing and needs no special case: an invisible child is skipped and its space reclaimed. A menu supplies the right icon on its own (control.declare). The fill walks the four-rung ladder — control at rest, controlHover, controlPressed, and controlSelected while its menu is open — so hovering a button never looks like pressing it.

entries.title: Button.baseline
entries.text: The baseline a row aligns this control by — its label's, in the control's own coordinates. A SimpleLayout or WrappingLayout with align = baseline sits the button's text on the same line as a neighbouring Text or Markdown; without this declaration the layout would refuse the button by name (a baseline is claimed, never guessed from a box). Declared here so every button carries it; an icon-only button still answers its (invisible) label's line. row: View [ layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 10, align = baseline ], Text [ fontSize = 18, text = "Ready?" ], Button [ label = "Save", primary = true ] // its label sits on the text's line ] number

entries.title: Button.label
entries.text: The button's text. "" (the default) leaves it iconless-and-wordless, which is only useful with an icon — a button with neither has nothing to press. string

entries.title: Button.primary
entries.text: Marks this as the affirmative action: it fills with the accent — accentHover and accentPressed as the pointer hovers and presses — and takes theme.accentText for its ink. One per group of choices — a dialog's Save, not its Cancel. Purely a style decision; it changes nothing about behaviour. Button [ label = "Cancel" ], Button [ label = "Save", primary = true ] boolean

entries.title: Button.gap
entries.text: Space between the icon and the label, when both are present. number

entries.title: Button.padH
entries.text: Horizontal padding inside the button, each side. The button sizes to its content plus twice this, so widening it is how you make a short label less cramped. Button [ label = "OK", padH = 28 ] // a short word, given room Button [ label = "Add", iconLeft = "PlusIcon", gap = 12 ] number

entries.title: Button.inkColor
entries.text: The one ink decision, so a button's icon and its label always agree: the accent text colour when primary, the ordinary text colour otherwise. textColor follows it. Override this rather than textColor alone, or the icon and the words drift apart. class DangerButton extends Button [ inkColor = { primary ? white : crimson } ] Color

entries.title: Button.height
entries.text: The theme decides, when it has an opinion: theme.buttonHeight sets it (a platform theme's native control height); a theme that leaves it unset gets 40. A height at the use site overrides both. Length

entries.title: Button.cornerRadius
entries.text: A theme that rounds buttons by a fixed radius sets theme.buttonRadius; it is capped at half the height, so a short button goes fully pill without a squared corner. Otherwise the shared controlRadius every control uses. Radius

entries.title: Button.width
entries.text: Content-sized: the run — icon, label, icon — plus padH each side. Give it a width and the run centres inside it, so a dialog's equal-width row keeps every label centred. Length

entries.title: Button.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole control, icon and label alike, rather than recolouring it — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none. number

entries.title: Button.fill
entries.text: The state ladder, one rung per interaction fact, first match wins: an open menu holds the selected tint, so the button stays lit while its menu is up; pressed beats hovered; at rest, the quiet control. A primary button climbs the same ladder in the accent: held — pressed, or its menu open — is accentPressed, hovered is accentHover, at rest accent. Every rung is a theme token, so a theme restyles every button's states at once; a platform whose controls do not answer a passing pointer states its hover tones equal to its rest tones (Cupertino does). Fill

entries.title: Button.stroke
entries.text: A hairline only where the theme wants one: themes that border their secondary buttons set theme.buttonBorder; flat themes leave it null and get no stroke. A primary button is never bordered — the accent fill is its edge. Stroke

entries.title: Button.press
entries.text: The activation path, called by a click and by Space/Enter. It flashes the press tint, opens an attached menu if there is one, then calls onClick. Override onClick for ordinary use; override this only to change what activation means. press()

entries.title: Button.click
entries.text: Your handler. Fires after the press is delivered, so the affordance has already run — put the work here, not in press(). onClick()

entries.title: TextLabel
entries.text: A Text that centers its ink in its parent's height — the vertical placement a label wants, as opposed to a paragraph. Use it for the text inside a control or any centered caption; use plain Text for flowing copy. Why it exists. y = center on a plain Text centers the geometric box (the ordinary meaning, matching every other view). But a label sitting in a box wants its letterforms optically centered, not the font's box with its asymmetric ascent/descent leading — otherwise the text reads a hair low. TextLabel supplies a y that centers the cap band (cap-top to baseline), the optical centre for a label: y = { parent.height / 2 - this.baseline + this.capHeight / 2 } That expression cap-centres the label: the ink sits centred by its cap band rather than by its box, which is what reads as centred for a label. It is written out here, once, instead of at every use site. It is a plain constraint over the Text's own live metric facts (baseline, capHeight, measured from the effective font), so it re-centers when the font, the size, or the parent's height changes. Override y on an instance to opt out. The centre is the cap band because that is what the platform control themes (Cupertino, Mountain View, Redmond) are matched against.

entries.title: TextLabel.y
entries.text: Centres the ink on the parent's height by its cap band — baseline and cap height — rather than by the line box, which is what a label beside a control wants and a paragraph does not. Length

entries.title: Switch
entries.text: A boolean control with a sliding thumb — same value contract as Checkbox (checked, input owns the destination), different body language: the thumb springs between its two rest points, so toggling moves rather than jumps.

entries.title: Switch.checked
entries.text: Whether the switch is on. Constrain it (checked = { app.muted }) and override input to own the destination, or leave it and read it back — a Switch works standalone with no wiring. boolean

entries.title: Switch.width
entries.text: A theme with a native switch size says so (theme.switchWidth); otherwise 44, the common pill. Length

entries.title: Switch.height
entries.text: A theme with a native switch size says so (theme.switchHeight); otherwise 24. Length

entries.title: Switch.cornerRadius
entries.text: Always a pill — half the height, whatever the height is. Radius

entries.title: Switch.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole control — every part alike, never a recolour — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none: the one place the number lives. number

entries.title: Switch.fill
entries.text: The track's ladder for a toggle: checked takes the accent; unchecked shows the selected tint while hovered or pressed and the quiet control tint at rest — so the track answers the pointer before the value flips. Fill

entries.title: Switch.stroke
entries.text: A hairline in the accent when checked, in the theme's line colour otherwise, so the track keeps an edge on light and dark surfaces alike. Stroke

entries.title: Switch.input
entries.text: Where the value goes. The default writes checked; override it and the switch becomes a delivery mechanism for state you own. press() never writes checked directly, so a constrained switch never fights its constraint. input(v)

entries.title: Switch.press
entries.text: Toggles, by delivering the flipped value through input. Called by a click and by Space/Enter. press()

entries.title: Switch.click
entries.text: Fires on click when the switch is enabled. press() is the activation path; prefer overriding input if what you want is the value. onClick()

entries.title: Slider
entries.text: A bounded number by drag. Same value contract as every control — value is the attribute, input owns the destination (default: itself) — and the delivery is continuous during a drag. Pressing the track jumps to that position (local coordinates); the drag then follows the pointer by root-space delta (app.pointerX), so it survives the pointer leaving the control. Arrow keys nudge by step. col: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ], vol: Slider [ value = 40 ], Text [ text = { volume ${Math.round(vol.value)} } ] ]

entries.title: Slider.value
entries.text: Where the handle sits, in your own units. Standalone the slider owns it; constrained (value = { app.volume }) it needs an input override with it, or the drag's own delivery is refused against the constraint. number

entries.title: Slider.min
entries.text: The value at the left end. number

entries.title: Slider.max
entries.text: The value at the right end. number

entries.title: Slider.step
entries.text: The quantum every delivered value snaps to, and the distance one arrow key moves. step = 0.01 for a fine continuous control; it is never zero — the quantizer divides by it. number

entries.title: Slider.frac
entries.text: The handle's position as 0…1, derived from the value and the range. What the track, fill, and thumb all position from; read it to hang your own decoration off the handle. number

entries.title: Slider.dragging
entries.text: True from pointer-down until the captured release. The pressed intrinsic deliberately will not do here — it is hit-chain-based, so it goes false the moment the pointer leaves the thumb, while a drag must survive exactly that. boolean

entries.title: Slider.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Slider.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Slider.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole control — every part alike, never a recolour — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none: the one place the number lives. number

entries.title: Slider.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the circular grabber — the part the arrow keys move — rather than the whole track. focusShape()

entries.title: Slider.input
entries.text: Where the value goes, and it fires continuously through a drag, not once at release: the owner decides what to do with the stream, and the data layer owns any coalescing. Override it to redirect the value (input(v: number) { app.volume = v }); the default writes value. input(v)

entries.title: Slider.quant
entries.text: Snaps a raw value to step and clamps it into min…max. Every delivery routes through it, so an override changes what the slider can produce — logarithmic scales, detents, a magnetic centre. quant(v)

entries.title: Slider.barStyle
entries.text: True when the theme asks for the Material-3 rendition: a vertical bar handle with the track shortened either side of it rather than drawn through. One theme token (theme.sliderHandle) selects a rendition — data, not a fork. barStyle()

entries.title: Slider.dotStyle
entries.text: True for the Fluent rendition: a round grabber with an accent dot inside that grows under hover and press. The other value of the same token. dotStyle()

entries.title: Slider.pointerDown
entries.text: Jumps the value to the pressed position, claims focus, and latches the drag. onPointerDown(e)

entries.title: Slider.pointerUp
entries.text: Ends the drag. onPointerUp()

entries.title: Slider.pointerMove
entries.text: Tracks the drag by root-space pointer delta, so the handle keeps up with a pointer that has left the control. onPointerMove()

entries.title: Slider.keyDown
entries.text: Left and Right nudge by one step, delivered through input like any other change. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: RadioGroup
entries.text: One-of-N. Radios are written as the group's direct children — the group's layout arranges them, and each radio reaches its group as parent: RadioGroup [ value = "m", input(v: string) { app.size = v }, Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ], Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ], Radio [ choice = "l", label = "Large" ], ] size: RadioGroup [ x = 20, y = 20, value = "m", Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ], Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ], Radio [ choice = "l", label = "Large" ] ]

entries.title: RadioGroup.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record this widget styles off — a provided value (the app provides it once with App [ theme = { … } ]; Control and the library widgets read it). Reads theme.accent and its kin as typed members; defaults to the house look. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: RadioGroup.value
entries.text: The group's value — the chosen choice, and the only value slot in the pair. A Radio has none of its own; it derives on from this. Standalone the group owns it; constrained, override input beside it as with any control. string

entries.title: RadioGroup.input
entries.text: Where the choice goes. The default writes value; override it to own the destination (input(v: string) { app.size = v }) and the radios keep working untouched, because they deliver rather than store. input(v)

entries.title: RadioGroup.pick
entries.text: Selects a choice by name — the seam a Radio calls on its group. Call it to move the selection from code without bypassing input. pick(v)

entries.title: Radio
entries.text: One choice in a RadioGroup: a direct child of the group, naming itself with choice. A radio stores nothing — it derives on from the group's value and delivers its choice to the group when pressed, so turning one on can never leave another stale. App [ width = 300, height = 120, fill = white, textColor = black, size: string = "m", RadioGroup [ x = 20, y = 20, value = { app.size }, input(v: string) { app.size = v }, Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ], Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ] ], Text [ x = 160, y = 20, text = { "size: " + app.size } ] ]

entries.title: Radio.baseline
entries.text: The baseline a row aligns this radio by — its caption's, so a row of mixed controls and text under align = baseline reads as one line. number

entries.title: Radio.choice
entries.text: This radio's identity within its group, compared against the group's value by string. Required and unique per group — two radios sharing a choice light together. string

entries.title: Radio.label
entries.text: The text beside the dot. "" renders the dot alone. string

entries.title: Radio.on
entries.text: Whether this radio is the group's current choice. Derived from the group, never stored — which is why turning one on cannot leave another stale. boolean

entries.title: Radio.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Radio.width
entries.text: Content-sized: the dot, then a gap and the label when there is one. A label-less radio is exactly its dot. Length

entries.title: Radio.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole choice, dot and label alike — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none. number

entries.title: Radio.focusShape
entries.text: Rings the round dot rather than the dot-plus-label row. focusShape()

entries.title: Radio.press
entries.text: Delivers this radio's choice to the group. Called by a click and by Space/Enter. press()

entries.title: Radio.click
entries.text: Runs press() when enabled. onClick()

entries.title: Field
entries.text: A labeled form row: the label column, then whatever control the use site nests (its direct child, arranged by the row's layout): Field [ label = "Name", TextInput [ width = 220, height = 30 ] ] labelWidth is the shared-column knob. form: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ], Field [ label = "Name", TextInput [ width = 200, height = 28 ] ], Field [ label = "Notify", Switch [ ] ] ]

entries.title: Field.baseline
entries.text: The baseline a row aligns this field by — its caption's. Two fields side by side under align = baseline keep their captions on one line whatever their controls' heights. number

entries.title: Field.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record this widget styles off — a provided value (the app provides it once with App [ theme = { … } ]; Control and the library widgets read it). Reads theme.accent and its kin as typed members; defaults to the house look. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: Field.label
entries.text: The caption in the left column. It is a Text, not a control's own label — a Field labels whatever you nest, so the nested control's own label should usually be empty or you will render the words twice. string

entries.title: Field.labelWidth
entries.text: The label column's width, and the knob that aligns a form. Every row in a form sets the same plain number — one value, repeated or read from a shared attribute (labelWidth = { app.formLabels }). It is deliberately not measured from the widest label: aggregating over sibling rows is exactly what the constraint system refuses, so the shared column is a value you state rather than one the form discovers. number

entries.title: ProgressBar
entries.text: Display-only bounded number — the read-only sibling of Slider (same value/ min/max vocabulary, no interaction, no input). Restyle by theme; set width at the use site (220 by default).

entries.title: ProgressBar.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record this widget styles off — a provided value (the app provides it once with App [ theme = { … } ]; Control and the library widgets read it). Reads theme.accent and its kin as typed members; defaults to the house look. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: ProgressBar.value
entries.text: Where the bar sits, in the units you choose. Clamped into min…max for display, so a value outside the range renders full or empty rather than overflowing. number

entries.title: ProgressBar.min
entries.text: The value that reads as empty. Defaults to 0. number

entries.title: ProgressBar.max
entries.text: The value that reads as full. Defaults to 100 — set it to your own total and pass raw counts as value rather than converting to a percentage yourself. number

entries.title: ProgressBar.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: ProgressBar.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: ProgressBar.cornerRadius
entries.text: Radius

entries.title: ProgressBar.fill
entries.text: The track wears the quiet control tint; the filled part is the bar's own child in the accent, so a theme restyles both at once. Fill

entries.title: FocusRing
entries.text: The travelling focus indicator: a shape-hugging rounded outline that flies to the focused control and reshapes to its own silhouette on arrival. The ring springs position, size and cornerRadius together, which is why a Radio's row ring, a pill Switch's ring and a text field's ring each differ — the targets do. The model: The fact — the ring listens to Focus (a Focus [ onFocusChange(v: View) { … } ] member) and tracks the target's root-space geometry on every change, pointer or keyboard. A pointer focus parks the ring there silently (snap, no show) — so the next Tab's flight departs from the control the user just clicked, never from a stale perch. Roles, theme-elected — theme.focusRing: "both" (or true, the default) · "travel" (flight, then an idle fade) · "rest" (no flight — the ring appears in place and stays) · false (no ring; the theme's components carry the at-rest indication — the invariant lives with the theme-and-components pair). While keyboard modality holds and the role includes rest, the ring rests — no idle fade; a pointer press clears modality and the ring hides (web :focus-visible semantics). The flight is the flourish — theme.focusAnimate = false snaps every move; the underdamped travel is default-on. It arrives automatically with any Control-descended component; declare your own FocusRing [ ] (or subclass) to replace it. Pure chrome: never focusable, never a pointer target. The silhouette is the target's focusShape() when it declares one, else its bounds at its cornerRadius. You do not instantiate this, and you do not position it. Tab between the controls below and watch it fly; the members exist for a subclass that replaces the rendition, and for the theme tokens that elect its behaviour. row: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 12 ], Button [ label = "One" ], Button [ label = "Two" ], Checkbox [ label = "Three" ] ]

entries.title: FocusRing.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record this widget styles off — a provided value (the app provides it once with App [ theme = { … } ]; Control and the library widgets read it). Reads theme.accent and its kin as typed members; defaults to the house look. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: FocusRing.overlayUp
entries.text: True while an overlay owns the keyboard (an open Menu). The ring stands down — the menu's own rover is the focus story, and a page ring poking around a panel reads as chrome fighting chrome. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.shown
entries.text: Whether the ring is visible. A pointer focus parks it silently — geometry current, ring hidden — so the next Tab departs from the control the user just clicked rather than from a stale perch. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.placed
entries.text: Whether the ring has ever had a target to park on. The first appearance never flies, because a flight from nowhere is a streak across the app. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.idle
entries.text: True once a travel-role ring has sat still long enough to fade out. A resting ring never sets it. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.opacity
entries.text: number

entries.title: FocusRing.visible
entries.text: Visible while its faded opacity still shows anything, and never while an overlay is up — a ring behind a dialog would point at something you cannot reach. boolean

entries.title: FocusRing.pointerEvents
entries.text: string

entries.title: FocusRing.ringRole
entries.text: The theme's election, from theme.focusRing: "both" (the default), "travel" (flight, then fading once it settles), "rest" (appears in place and stays, no flight), or "off". "off" is legitimate only when the theme's own controls carry an at-rest focus indication — the invariant belongs to the theme-and-components pair, not to the ring alone. ringRole()

entries.title: FocusRing.restRole
entries.text: Whether the elected role includes resting — a resting ring does not idle-fade. restRole()

entries.title: FocusRing.travelRole
entries.text: Whether the elected role includes the flight. travelRole()

entries.title: FocusRing.snapTo
entries.text: Lands the ring on its target immediately, skipping the flight. What a pointer focus, a first appearance, and theme.focusAnimate = false all use — and what a target moving under a resting ring uses , so a dragged slider thumb carries the ring rigidly instead of springing after it. snapTo()

entries.title: FocusRing.draw
entries.text: Renders the outline: four corner arcs with arms whose length is a pure function of distance from the target, so the physics does the choreography. Override to replace the rendition entirely. theme.focusSights = true restores the open-bracket "target sights" reading; theme.focusRingInnerWidth adds the Fluent two-tone band. draw(d)

entries.title: Accordion
entries.text: Stacked pane headers with one pane open at a time, each pane sliding open and closed on a spring over its height. The load-bearing mechanic: a pane's content is present through the whole open and close , revealed and concealed by the pane's own clip as its height animates. That is what makes the motion read as a pane opening rather than as content appearing — never an instant pop, never a blank gap. The open pane is one attribute on the group — value, the open pane's name — which is exactly RadioGroup's shape. Panes are the group's direct children; each names itself (name, defaulting to its label) and derives open from the group. Content is authored as the Pane's ordinary children — the Pane stacks its header then the content, and clips. The pane stacks them flush, header against content, because the header is edge-to-edge and an inset that reached it would break that. So the breathing room around a pane's content is the content's own padding: Accordion [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, Pane [ label = "Account", initial = true, View [ width = 100%, padding = 12, Text [ width = 100%, wrap = true, text = "Panes slide on a spring; the content rides the whole way." ] ] ], Pane [ label = "Privacy", View [ width = 100%, padding = 12, Text [ width = 100%, text = "One pane open at a time." ] ] ] ]

entries.title: Accordion.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record this widget styles off — a provided value (the app provides it once with App [ theme = { … } ]; Control and the library widgets read it). Reads theme.accent and its kin as typed members; defaults to the house look. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: Accordion.value
entries.text: The open pane's name — the group's whole value, exactly RadioGroup's shape. Assign it to open a pane from code; "" closes all of them. A Pane never stores whether it is open, it derives it from here, which is why the one-open-at-a-time invariant cannot break. string

entries.title: Pane
entries.text: One pane of an Accordion: a header you press and the content you write as its ordinary children. A pane derives open from the group's value — it never stores it — and slides open and closed on a spring over its height, its content present the whole way and revealed by the pane's own clip. App [ width = 300, height = 180, fill = white, textColor = black, Accordion [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, Pane [ label = "Details", initial = true, Text [ width = 100%, padding = 12, text = { "open: " + parent.open } ] ], Pane [ label = "More", Text [ padding = 12, text = "Press a header." ] ] ] ]

entries.title: Pane.label
entries.text: The pane header's text, and — unless you set name — its identity in the group. string

entries.title: Pane.name
entries.text: This pane's identity, defaulting to its label. Set it when two panes share a label, or when the label is user-facing copy you expect to change , so the group's value does not move under you when the wording does. string

entries.title: Pane.initial
entries.text: Seeds the group: the first pane declaring initial = true opens if nothing else has claimed value yet. A one-shot at init, not a constraint — to drive which pane is open from state, constrain the group's value instead . boolean

entries.title: Pane.open
entries.text: Whether this pane is the group's current one. Derived; read it to style your content. boolean

entries.title: Pane.twist
entries.text: The header chevron's angle, in radians, sprung between 0 and −π/2. It turns in step with the height animation rather than snapping , which is the whole reason it is a number and not a swap between two marks — a number can be sprung. number

entries.title: Pane.width
entries.text: A pane is as wide as its accordion; only its height is its own. Length

entries.title: Pane.clip
entries.text: Shape

entries.title: Pane.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole pane, header and content alike, rather than recolouring it — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none. A disabled pane neither opens nor closes; whatever it shows stays as it is. number

entries.title: Pane.tabOrder
entries.text: Contributes the pane's contents to keyboard traversal only while it is open. A closed pane is clip-occluded rather than hidden — its content must stay visible for the slide to carry it — so this is what stops Tab from descending into a pane the user cannot see . The header itself remains a stop either way. tabOrder()

entries.title: Pane.press
entries.text: Opens this pane by writing its name to the group. Called by a click and by Space/Enter on the header. press()

entries.title: Pane.init
entries.text: Applies initial. Fires once per pane. onInit()

entries.title: Pane.click
entries.text: Runs press() when enabled. onClick()

entries.title: Tooltip
entries.text: The layer system's floor: any view sets tip = "…" and this singleton renders it — hover delay, placement, flip, and theming are nobody's problem at the use site. It arrives automatically when any view in the program carries a tip, as FocusRing does; declare your own Tooltip [ ] (or subclass) to replace the rendition. It listens to the Tip service (a Tip [ onTip(e: TipEvent) { … } ] member), which owns the platform conventions (the show delay — tooltipDelay, ~1s in the Cupertino and Redmond conventions, ~500ms MountainView — instant retarget while showing, hide on press). Placement is theme data too (tooltipPlacement): "below" (the default — under the target, centered, flipping above at the edge), "above" (flipping below), or "pointer" (the Cupertino help tag — offset below-right of where the cursor rests). Always clamped inside the app. Pure chrome — never focusable, never a pointer target, always above content (the auto-splice puts it last in the App, and source order stacks). Theming (the four cities carry the tokens): tooltipBg / tooltipText / tooltipLine (null = no border) / tooltipSize (11 in Cupertino, 12 elsewhere). Cupertino and Redmond wear bordered surface chips; San Francisco and Mountain View the inverse chip. You do not instantiate this. Set tip on any view and the singleton appears; the members below exist for a subclass that replaces the rendition. View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 130, height = 38, cornerRadius = 8, fill = steelblue, tip = "Saves your changes", Text [ x = center, y = center, textColor = white, text = "Save" ] ]

entries.title: Tooltip.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record this widget styles off — a provided value (the app provides it once with App [ theme = { … } ]; Control and the library widgets read it). Reads theme.accent and its kin as typed members; defaults to the house look. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: Tooltip.tipText
entries.text: The text currently displayed, pushed in by the Tip service from the hovered view's tip. A subclass reads this; nothing writes it from app code. string

entries.title: Tooltip.shown
entries.text: Whether a tip is currently up. Driven by the service's delay, retarget and hide rules — not by you. boolean

entries.title: Tooltip.placement
entries.text: Where the chip sits, elected by theme.tooltipPlacement: "below" (the default, centred under the target, flipping above at the edge), "above" (the Fluent default, flipping below), or "pointer" (the Cupertino help tag, offset below-right of the resting cursor). Always clamped inside the app. string

entries.title: Tooltip.visible
entries.text: Shown only when asked and there is text to show — an empty tip never paints a bare box. boolean

entries.title: Tooltip.width
entries.text: Sized to its text plus padding, so the box fits the words and never the other way round. Length

entries.title: Tooltip.height
entries.text: Sized to its text plus padding, one line or several. Length

entries.title: Tooltip.x
entries.text: Beside the pointer, or centred under the element, then clamped inside the app with a 4px margin — a tip near an edge slides in rather than clipping. Length

entries.title: Tooltip.y
entries.text: Below the pointer, or below or above the element as placement says, flipping to the other side when the preferred one would leave the app. Length

entries.title: Tooltip.cornerRadius
entries.text: Radius

entries.title: Tooltip.fill
entries.text: The theme's tooltip ground when it names one, else a dark slate — a tip is the one surface that stays dark on a light theme. Fill

entries.title: Tooltip.stroke
entries.text: A hairline only when the theme names a tooltip line; flat themes get none. Stroke

entries.title: Tooltip.pointerEvents
entries.text: string

entries.title: Menu
entries.text: The record-driven menu: items are data — the component arranges; the author never composes rows. The standard record covers real OS menus: { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props?, minWidth? } key renders right-aligned — display only; the menu registers no shortcut. icon: "ClassName" names an icon class for the leading column, and the label shifts right to make room — the same vocabulary Segmented's choices use. One field covers every mark, including the ones no font gives you; a computed name needs its class kept with use [ Name ], since no static reference reaches it. enabled: false dims the row (theme.disabledOpacity) and refuses pick. { divider: true } is a separator line. submenu: [ …records… ] marks a cascade (the ▸ arrow). kind: "ClassName" renders the row's content with a named author class (app.createView — keep data-only classes with use [ Name ]), passed props as its datapath context. Behavior stays the row's: highlight, pick, keyboard are the menu's, always. minWidth is the room a row needs when it has no label to measure — a kind: row's own content. The panel is at least this wide; a longer label elsewhere still wins. Only a custom row needs it. Declared once, opened by many: rows carry onContextMenu(e) { app.rowMenu.openAt(this, e) }; the menu's items constraint derives from opener — per-row variation with zero per-row instances, live while open. openAt point-positions (the context-menu rule); openFor drops below a control (the attached-menu rule); both raise the menu (promotion — order is a slot) and clamp inside the app. Dismissal: the backdrop (a full-app child under the panel) — a press outside closes and is swallowed, the Mac rule; Escape closes; pick closes after delivery. App [ width = 320, height = 130, chose: string = "", edit: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut", key: "⌘X" }), ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy", key: "⌘C", checked: true }), ({ divider: true }), ({ id: "paste", label: "Paste", enabled: false }) ] }, picked(id: string) { app.chose = id } ], Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Edit", menu = { app.edit } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ] ]

entries.title: Menu.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record this widget styles off — a provided value (the app provides it once with App [ theme = { … } ]; Control and the library widgets read it). Reads theme.accent and its kin as typed members; defaults to the house look. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: Menu.widestLabel
entries.text: The widest row label, measured — the content the panel's width is built from. number

entries.title: Menu.widestKey
entries.text: The widest key equivalent, measured; zero when no row carries one, which is what decides whether the key column exists. number

entries.title: Menu.hasSubs
entries.text: Whether any row opens a submenu — a cascade arrow needs its own trailing room. boolean

entries.title: Menu.widestCustom
entries.text: The widest minWidth any row asks for. A kind: row renders its own content and has no label to measure, so it states the room it needs in its record and the panel is at least that wide; a longer label elsewhere still wins. number

entries.title: Menu.minWidth
entries.text: The narrowest a menu gets, whatever its rows measure — a two-item menu of short words still reads as a menu. number

entries.title: Menu.items
entries.text: The rows, as records — never children. A menu arranges its own rows, so handing it views is not merely discouraged, there is nowhere to put them. The record is { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props?, minWidth? }; a plain array is fine (no Dataset required). Because it is an ordinary attribute it can be a constraint — derive it from opener and one menu serves every row of a table , live while it is open. array

entries.title: Menu.opener
entries.text: The view this menu was opened for, set by openAt/openFor and cleared on close. The key to declaring one menu and opening it from many places: read it in the items constraint to vary the rows per opener, with no per-opener instance. View

entries.title: Menu.shown
entries.text: Whether the menu is up. Read it; open through openAt/openFor rather than assigning it , or the menu appears unplaced, unraised, and without its keyboard claim. Closing by assignment skips the cascade teardown for the same reason. boolean

entries.title: Menu.hasIcons
entries.text: Whether any row carries an icon — which is what decides the icon gutter exists at all. A menu with no icons has no gutter, and the text edge moves accordingly. boolean

entries.title: Menu.hasChecks
entries.text: Whether any row can be checked — a record carrying checked, true or false — which is what decides the check column exists, exactly as AppKit reserves its state column for any item with a state image to draw. A menu of plain commands leads its text 17 in; one with a checkable row, 24. boolean

entries.title: Menu.checkW
entries.text: What the check column adds to the leading air when it exists (7 — the Mac's 25.5 vs 17.5, measured), else 0: the amount every column to its right shifts by. number

entries.title: Menu.textEdge
entries.text: The x every row's label starts at — one line for the whole menu, icons or not, and what a kind row must align its own content to. number

entries.title: Menu.isRoot
entries.text: False on a cascade child. The root owns the backdrop, the deferred delivery, and the Escape-closes-everything behaviour; a submenu delegates all three upward. boolean

entries.title: Menu.rootMenu
entries.text: The root of this menu's cascade chain — null on the root itself. Menu

entries.title: Menu.child
entries.text: The one lazily-created submenu instance, reused across every row that cascades. A Menu cannot declare a Menu child (it would recurse), so the cascade is built by name at first use. Menu

entries.title: Menu.activeRow
entries.text: The row the keyboard rover currently highlights, or null when the pointer is driving. Read-only in practice. View

entries.title: Menu.visible
