entries.text: Derived from shown, the menu's own open fact. Visibility is never set from outside — openAt and openFor set the fact, and dismissal clears it. boolean

entries.title: Menu.height
entries.text: As tall as its panel, which is as tall as its rows — capped just inside the app's height, past which the panel scrolls its rows and the rover keeps the landing row in view. Length

entries.title: Menu.width
entries.text: Follows the rows: the text edge, the widest label, then the key column or the trailing air — the metrics of a real macOS menu, measured (the longest label trails the edge by 18; a key column sits 26 clear of the longest label and ends 16 from the edge; menu bar menus and popups measure the same). A use site's own width overrides; minWidth floors it. Length

entries.title: Menu.picked
entries.text: The delivery seam — override it at the use site. Receives the picked row's id, and the id is the whole message. Called after the menu has left the screen, so a slow action can never freeze an open menu. picked(id)

entries.title: Menu.expectedHeight
entries.text: The panel's height before it has been laid out, measured when it exists and estimated from the record count when it does not. The flip-above decision cannot wait for a settle, which is why this exists. expectedHeight()

entries.title: Menu.openAt
entries.text: Opens the menu at the pointer, given the serving view and the pointer event — the context-menu rule. Clamped inside the app like any placement. ContextMenu wraps this as open. openAt(v, e)

entries.title: Menu.openFor
entries.text: Opens the menu anchored below a control, flipping above it when there is not room below and more room above — the native select discipline. The attached-menu rule; what Control.menu uses. openFor(v)

entries.title: Menu.place
entries.text: Positions the panel from root-space coordinates, converting into the parent's space and clamping inside the app — so a menu works declared at App level or inside a component. The chain offset is snapshotted at open: menu chrome does not move while a menu is up. place(x, y)

entries.title: Menu.close
entries.text: Takes the menu down, closes any cascade under it, and releases the keyboard claim. close()

entries.title: Menu.pick
entries.text: Delivers a row: dismisses first, then delivers, one painted frame later — the native menu contract, and the reason a long-running action cannot leave a menu stranded on screen. A submenu routes to the root so the whole chain closes as one. pick(id)

entries.title: Menu.openSub
entries.text: Opens a row's submenu, creating the shared child menu on first use and placing it alongside the row. openSub(row, subItems)

entries.title: Menu.closeSub
entries.text: Closes the cascade under this menu, if any. closeSub()

entries.title: Menu.rootClose
entries.text: Closes the entire chain from wherever it is called — what Escape and an outside press both do. rootClose()

entries.title: Menu.step
entries.text: Moves the keyboard rover by ±1 over the pickable rows, skipping dividers, disabled rows and custom-content rows, and scrolls the landing row into view. step(d)

entries.title: Menu.pickActive
entries.text: Picks the roved row — Enter's action. On a row with a submenu it enters the cascade instead. pickActive()

entries.title: Menu.enterSub
entries.text: Enters the roved row's submenu and puts the rover on its first row — ArrowRight's action. enterSub()

entries.title: MenuBar
entries.text: The record-driven menu bar: whole menus are data — menus = { [ ({ id, label, bold?, items: [ …menu records… ] }), … ] } — and the component arranges. One internal Menu serves every title; its items constraint derives from the open title's record, so item state (enabled, checked, labels) stays live while the menu is up. Because the records are the single declaration, an app can derive its key registry from the same array the bar renders — nothing is declared twice. Tracking is the classic desktop behavior: titles do not highlight on mere hover; a click opens (and highlights) a title; while any menu is open, moving across another title switches to it; clicking the open title closes. Delivery is the one seam: picked(id) — override at the use site. A dropped menu paints over the bar's later siblings: the bar raises itself when a menu opens (stacking is source order, and raise() is the runtime verb for it). A bar nested inside a container that sits under other content wants that container declared last, or a menu hosted at the app layer as Combobox does. App [ width = 380, height = 190, chose: string = "", bar: MenuBar [ x = 12, y = 8, menus = { [ ({ id: "file", label: "File", items: [ ({ id: "new", label: "New", key: "⌘N" }), ({ id: "open", label: "Open…" }) ] }), ({ id: "edit", label: "Edit", items: [ ({ id: "undo", label: "Undo" }), ({ divider: true }), ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut" }) ] }) ] }, picked(id: string) { app.chose = id } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 70, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ] ]

entries.title: MenuBar.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record this widget styles off — a provided value (the app provides it once with App [ theme = { … } ]; Control and the library widgets read it). Reads theme.accent and its kin as typed members; defaults to the house look. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: MenuBar.menus
entries.text: The whole bar as data: [ { id, label, bold?, kind?, items: [ …menu records… ] } ], where items is exactly Menu's record shape. One internal Menu serves every title , deriving its rows from the open one — so item state stays live while a menu is up, and there is nothing to keep in step. Because the records are the single declaration, an app can derive its keyboard-shortcut registry from the same array the bar renders. array

entries.title: MenuBar.ink
entries.text: Overrides the titles' colour, for a bar drawn straight over a wallpaper where the platform text turns light. null uses the theme's text colour. The dropdown menus stay themed either way — this is the bar's own ink, not the menu's. Color

entries.title: MenuBar.openId
entries.text: Which title's menu is open, by id — "" when none is. string

entries.title: MenuBar.shown
entries.text: Whether any menu in the bar is currently open. boolean

entries.title: MenuBar.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: MenuBar.width
entries.text: Content-sized to its row of titles, so it sits in a chrome bar without a stated width. Length

entries.title: MenuBar.picked
entries.text: The delivery seam — override it at the use site. Receives the picked item's id from any menu in the bar; the id is the whole message. picked(id)

entries.title: MenuBar.openMenu
entries.text: Opens a title's menu and keeps the bar itself above the menu's backdrop, which is what lets tracking continue while a menu is up. openMenu(t)

entries.title: MenuBar.trackMenu
entries.text: Switches to another title while a menu is already open — bar tracking: titles do not highlight on mere hover, but once a menu is open, crossing another title opens that one. trackMenu(t)

entries.title: MenuBar.stepMenu
entries.text: Moves to the adjacent title's menu — Left/Right while a menu is open, yielding to the open menu when a submenu is up or the rover sits on one. stepMenu(d)

entries.title: Dialog
entries.text: The modal tier: a full-app scrim that swallows every press — modal input blocking, no light dismiss — under a centered panel with a focus trap. Buttons are records (the records door): { id, label, default?, cancel? }, rendered as themed library Buttons right-aligned in the platform arrangement. Focus is saved on open and restored on close. Keyboard: Return picks the default button (the Cupertino rule; a focused button also activates on Space/Enter — the pick guard makes the double harmless), Escape picks the cancel record when one exists, else just closes. The idioms — one verb each, an optional callback receiving the picked id (the picked(id) override remains the declarative seam): dlg.notice("Saved", "Your changes were saved.") dlg.ask("Save changes?", "Unsaved changes will be lost.", (id) => …) dlg.error("Could not connect", "The server refused the connection.") ask is Cancel / No / Yes-default; error renders the title in the theme's errorColor. Platform structure is data: dialogWidth, dialogButtons = "end" (a right-aligned row — San Francisco, Material) "stack" (the stacked alert — full-width buttons stacked, default on top) "fill" (WinUI ContentDialog — equal-width buttons filling the row), dialogAlign = "left" "center" (the Cupertino centered title), dialogTitleSize / dialogBodySize. Plus scrimColor + scrimOpacity (Cupertino barely dims — alerts separate by shadow; Material's scrim is 32%; Fluent's smoke 30%), the menuShadow family, errorColor. Declare one and call it. A Dialog is not a view you show and hide around your content — it is a standing member you open with a verb, so the same instance serves every prompt in the program. App [ width = 520, height = 260, said: string = "", dlg: Dialog [ ], Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Delete…", onClick() { app.dlg.ask("Delete this file?", "This cannot be undone.", (id) => { app.said = id }) } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.said == "" ? "—" : "you chose: " + app.said } ] ]

entries.title: Dialog.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record this widget styles off — a provided value (the app provides it once with App [ theme = { … } ]; Control and the library widgets read it). Reads theme.accent and its kin as typed members; defaults to the house look. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: Dialog.shown
entries.text: Whether the dialog is up. Read it; open through a verb (ask, notice, error, open) rather than assigning it, or you get a panel with no buttons, no saved focus, and no focus trap engaged. boolean

entries.title: Dialog.title
entries.text: The heading. Set by the verbs; read it if you are restyling. string

entries.title: Dialog.message
entries.text: The body text under the title. "" hides the line entirely rather than leaving a gap. string

entries.title: Dialog.tone
entries.text: "error" tints the title with the theme's error colour; "" is the ordinary tone. string

entries.title: Dialog.buttons
entries.text: The button records currently rendered, in authored order. The "stack" arrangement reorders them for display — default on top, cancel at the bottom — without touching this. array

entries.title: Dialog.arrangement
entries.text: How the buttons lay out, elected by theme.dialogButtons: "end" (a right-aligned row), "stack" (full-width buttons stacked, Cupertino-style, default on top), or "fill" (equal-width buttons filling the row). Platform structure is data, not a fork. string

entries.title: Dialog.centered
entries.text: Whether the title and message are centre-aligned, elected by theme.dialogAlign. boolean

entries.title: Dialog.visible
entries.text: Derived from shown; open and close by the fact, never by assigning visibility. boolean

entries.title: Dialog.x
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Dialog.y
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Dialog.width
entries.text: A dialog is the whole app: its box is the backdrop and the panel is its child, so a press anywhere outside the panel lands on the dialog. Length

entries.title: Dialog.height
entries.text: The whole app's height, for the same reason as width. Length

entries.title: Dialog.picked
entries.text: The declarative delivery seam — override it at the use site. Receives the picked button's id. Fires after the dialog has left the screen, and in addition to any callback passed to the verb, so you may use either or both. picked(id)

entries.title: Dialog.open
entries.text: The general form the three idioms are built on: title, message, your own button records, a tone ("error" or ""), and an optional callback. Reach for it when the three idioms do not spell your choices — button records are { id, label, default?, cancel? } , and the two flags are what Return and Escape key off. open(t, m, btns, tone_, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.notice
entries.text: A single-OK acknowledgement. Delivers "ok". notice(t, m, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.error
entries.text: A single-OK acknowledgement with the title in the theme's error colour. Delivers "ok". error(t, m, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.ask
entries.text: The three-way prompt: Cancel / No / Yes, with Yes as the default. Delivers "cancel", "no" or "yes". ask(t, m, cb_)

entries.title: Dialog.close
entries.text: Takes the dialog down without delivering anything, and restores focus to whatever held it before. Focus is restored one turn later, deliberately — an immediate restore hands the in-flight keystroke back to the opener, which re-activates and reopens. close()

entries.title: Dialog.pick
entries.text: Delivers a button by id: dismisses first, then delivers, one painted frame later — the same contract as Menu.pick, so a slow action cannot freeze the dialog on screen. Guarded against double activation, so a focused default button answering Space and Return is harmless. pick(id)

entries.title: Dialog.focusDefault
entries.text: Puts keyboard focus on the default button when the dialog opens — or the last button when no record is marked default. focusDefault()

entries.title: Dialog.pickDefault
entries.text: Picks whichever button record carries default: true — Return's action, the Cupertino rule. pickDefault()

entries.title: Dialog.pickCancel
entries.text: Picks the cancel: true record when there is one, else just closes — Escape's action. A dialog with no cancel record still dismisses on Escape, it simply delivers nothing. pickCancel()

entries.title: AppIsland
entries.text: AppIsland embeds a live Declare application: give it a program and it mounts that program as its own child app — its own reactive graph, input router, and stage — sized to this view's box. There is no coordinate sync: the tenant fills the box, so your width/height constraints size it like any view. It composes DOMIsland (the sanctioned foreign-content leaf) and builds the host's mount key from structured inputs, so callers never hand-splice the run:… wire. The page host (browser/host-client.js) sees the key on the box, resolves the program on its boot ladder — prewarm → cache → in-browser compile, identical on the dev server and a static host — and renders the child. childName (inherited from DOMIsland) is the reverse channel: the running child's appName reflected back up, so a host can title itself by what it shows. The boundary What crosses an island says its direction (the guide's Embedding chapter). DOWN: list names in provides = ["dark", "base"], and the tenant reads each with hostProvided("dark", false) — a value resolves at the island as provided() does, the island's own attribute first, then its ancestors' provisions. UP: the tenant lists names in its App's exposes = ["docH"], and the host reads them with island.exposed("docH", 0). Both are reactive, per settle, with no handshake to write. post(topic, payload) / onPost(m: IslandPost) carry the verbs. The window frame, activation, and titling belong to the caller — a desktop window adds an onPointerDown that raises itself and reads childName for its title; the homepage and the viewer just size the box. This primitive is only the embedding.

entries.title: AppIsland.program
entries.text: What to run: a program name, a relative path ("../../calendar/calendar" reaches the real app — no copy of the source, ever), or the reserved "raw" live-edit channel, where the running program is the host app's liveSource and recompiles as it changes. "" detaches the island and nothing mounts, which is how a closed panel stops paying for its tenant — and what bounds the recursion when a program embeds a view of itself. The tenant runs in the host page's runtime, as its own app. Where its compiled program comes from is the host's arrangement: on the distro, a prewarmed artifact or a compile; in a production build, an artifact declarec made ahead of time — for every island whose program is a literal, and for every name the program declares in its ship [ islands = [ "name", … ] ] when the value is computed. A build carries no compiler unless the program declares ship [ compiler = true ], so an island naming a program the build did not produce reports that, with the fix, rather than mounting nothing. string

entries.title: AppIsland.slot
entries.text: The host's slot marker, derived from program — run:<program> — which is what the island host wires. Nothing to set by hand. string

entries.title: SimpleLayout
entries.text: The stacking idiom: siblings placed one after another along axis, in child order, spacing apart (negative overlaps). The cross axis and all sizes stay the children's own — a child centers itself across a row with the ordinary y = center. Invisible children are skipped and their space reclaimed; a skipped child still gets the slot it would occupy, so re-showing it needs no special case. A Spacer child flexes to absorb the run's slack along the axis (between two groups it pushes them apart; one on each side centers the run). Written in Declare over the Layout kernel: the whole strategy is this one pure place() — one box per laid child, aligned by index. Padding is the view's (View.padding), and this stack obeys it without knowing it exists: it arranges inside the room the view gives it, so a run placed at 0 starts at the content origin, the cross-axis band align works in is the room between the insets, and a view that sizes itself from the stack grows by both. The inset reaches every child, on both axes, align = none included — a child placing its own x = 0 sits on the content edge, not the view's, because the content box is the parent's and not this arrangement's. col: View [ x = 20, y = 20, layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ], View [ width = 160, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ], View [ width = 120, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ], View [ width = 190, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ] ]

entries.title: SimpleLayout.axis
entries.text: Which way children stack: y (the default) or x. A bare literal, not a string — axis = x, and note that x here is the axis token, not the position attribute. Axis

entries.title: SimpleLayout.spacing
entries.text: The gap between adjacent children. Negative overlaps them, which is how a stack of cards or avatars is built. number

entries.title: SimpleLayout.align
entries.text: The cross axis — y on a row, x on a stack. none (the default) leaves it to the children, who place themselves with the ordinary y = center. start center end aligns every child within the band: the view's own cross content extent — so a column width = 260 centres a width = { parent.width - 32 } child at 16, with the slack split evenly — falling back to the line, the tallest (widest) laid child's extent, on a view that derives its own cross size from these very children (reading an extent this arrangement feeds would be a cycle, and on such a view the line is that extent). A child wider than the band keeps the line, so it never hangs out both sides. baseline — a row only — sits every child on one baseline: a Text reports its own, and a composite declares which part carries it (baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }); a laid child that declares none is refused by name, at the child, and the checker says so before anything runs. A bare literal. CrossAlign

entries.title: SimpleLayout.place
entries.text: The whole strategy: one box per laid child, positioned along the axis in child order. Every size stays the children's own, and so does the cross axis unless align says otherwise — then the boxes carry that slot too, and own it. Override it in a subclass for custom geometry; a Layout's place() may aggregate over children, which is the one place that is allowed. place()

entries.title: WrappingLayout
entries.text: A horizontal flow that wraps: children run left to right spacing apart, and when the next one would overflow the view's width it drops to a new row, rowSpacing down. With room for one row it is a plain row; as the view narrows it stacks — cards that reflow on a phone with no media query. It owns both axes of each child (a flow is 2-D); sizes stay the children's own. justify sets each finished row along the flow — start, center, end, or fill, which spreads a row's slack into its gaps the way justified text does; indent and hangingIndent inset the first row and every row after it, the two shapes a paragraph takes. Division of labor: this is the tool for uniform, replicated collections that reflow by fitting. Managing named regions per width tier is ResponsiveLayout's. Written in Declare over the Layout kernel — the whole strategy is place(). Padding is the view's (View.padding), and a flow answers to it on both axes: rows wrap at the content width — the room between the left and right insets, never the view's own width — and a view that sizes itself from the flow grows by the vertical pair, so no row runs under the inset. box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 8, rowSpacing = 8 ], View [ width = 70, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ], View [ width = 110, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ], View [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ], View [ width = 120, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = darkslateblue ] ]

entries.title: WrappingLayout.spacing
entries.text: The horizontal gap between children in a row. number

entries.title: WrappingLayout.rowSpacing
entries.text: The vertical gap between rows. The two gaps are independent: a uniform grid writes the same number for both, and a negative rowSpacing pulls rows into each other, which is what a large display face wants when it wraps — the row height a big face reports is looser than the line wants to sit. number

entries.title: WrappingLayout.justify
entries.text: How a finished row sits along the flow: start (the default, left), center, end (right), or fill — the row's slack is spread evenly into the gaps between its children, so every full row ends flush at the right edge, as justified text does. As in text, the last row is left at start under fill (a ragged last line), and a row of one child has no gap to widen and stays put. A bare literal. Justify

entries.title: WrappingLayout.align
entries.text: Where each child sits within its row: start (the default — the row's top), center, end, or baseline, which sits every child in the row on one baseline — a Text reports its own, a composite declares which part carries it (baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }), and a child that declares none is refused by name and placed at the row's top. A row's height grows to hold the baseline-shifted children. When the flow never wrapped — one row, which is the whole content — center and end align it in the view's own height instead, so a single row in a height = 90 bar really sits in the middle of it; a view that derives its height from this flow keeps the row as the band. A bare literal. CrossAlign

entries.title: WrappingLayout.indent
entries.text: The first row's inset from the left, in pixels — a paragraph's first-line indent. The first row's usable width shrinks by it; later rows are unaffected (see hangingIndent). number

entries.title: WrappingLayout.hangingIndent
entries.text: The inset of every row after the first — a hanging indent, the shape of a bibliography entry or a wrapped signature whose continuation lines step in under the name. The two compose: indent sets where the first row starts, hangingIndent where the rest do. number

entries.title: WrappingLayout.place
entries.text: Runs the flow, wrapping when the next child would overflow the view's width. It owns both axes of each child — a flow is 2-D — while sizes stay the children's own. A child never wraps when it is first in its row, so one over-wide child overflows rather than looping forever. Each finished row starts at its indent, is justified along the flow, and has its children aligned across it, in one pass over the row. place()

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout
entries.text: A view's children often want one arrangement when there is room and another when there isn't: three panels side by side on a wide screen, the same panels stacked on a phone; an optional control that appears only when space allows. ResponsiveLayout states those alternatives directly. You give it a list of plans — each one says "from this width up, arrange the children like this" — and it keeps the right plan applied as the view's width changes. Hiding, showing, and dividing the width are all part of a plan, not separate wiring. bar: View [ layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [ { from: 900, flow: "row", share: { logo: 15, nav: 55, actions: 30 } }, { from: 600, flow: "row", share: { logo: 20, nav: 80, actions: 0 } }, { from: 0, flow: "stack" }, ] } ], logo: Logo [ ], nav: Nav [ ], actions: Actions [ ], ] Each entry's from means use this plan when the view is at least this wide — the entry with the largest from that fits wins, wherever it sits in the list, and an entry with from: 0 is the fallback for anything narrower. flow is the arrangement: "row" places children left to right; "stack" places them top to bottom. share divides width in either flow — in a row it apportions the run; in a stack it sets how wide each band is, as a plain percentage of the view. The names are the view's own child names, checked when the layout first arranges (a name with no child is a loud error). logo: 15 gives logo 15% of it; a share of 0 drops that child while the plan is active — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is just a number in the narrow plan, and they reappear by themselves when the view widens. gap sets the space between children (an entry may carry its own gap to override the layout's). Heights are never touched: children keep their own heights, and the view's height falls out of its content, as always. So the example reads as a storyboard: at 900 and up, a three-across row split 15/55/30; between 600 and 900, the actions drop and the nav takes their room; below 600, everything stacks. A plan need not name every child, and 20% means 20% of what is left. A child the plan leaves out keeps its natural width and the flow just places it — and the run a row's shares divide is what remains after the gaps and after those naturals . So a fixed-width logo beside two proportional regions composes without the author computing a percentage for the logo: layout: ResponsiveLayout [ gap = 10, plan = { [ { from: 0, flow: "row", share: { nav: 60, actions: 40 } }, ] } ], logo: View [ width = 200 ], // not named: keeps its 200 nav: Nav [ ], // 60% of what is left actions: Actions [ ], // 40% of what is left In an 880-wide bar that is 200 for the logo and 396 / 264 for the two regions — the row fills, exactly. Change the logo's width and the regions answer; they were never told about it. share: { logo: "auto" } says that out loud. The word means precisely what leaving the child out means — keep its natural size, divide the rest — so it buys no new geometry, only legibility: the plan reads as a complete statement of the row, and a name in a plan is checked against the tree, where an omission is mentioned nowhere. It is not share: 0, which is the opposite: 0 drops the child and reclaims its space, "auto" keeps the child at the size it chose for itself. In a stack "auto" is accepted and changes nothing — the flow axis there is height, which a share never touches. Two shares are refused, where the plan is read — both of them mistakes with no arrangement they could mean. A row's shares divide one run, so a row whose shares add to more than 100 is an error naming the plan and the total, rather than a row that runs its children off the end. And a share that is neither a number from 0 to 100 nor the word "auto" is an error naming the child, rather than a NaN width on it and a NaN position on its neighbours. The two things authors miss. share is not row-only: a "stack" entry may carry shares too, and they set each band's width — the narrow plan above could say { from: 0, flow: "stack", share: { logo: 100, nav: 100 } } to make both bands full-bleed. (A stack's shares are independent percentages of the view, not slices of one run, which is why two hundreds are fine there and a row's total is held to 100.) And share: 0 is the whole of "hide it when it's tight": a child dropped this way leaves the flow entirely and its space is reclaimed, so there is no reason to branch a tree on a width (narrow ? … : …) — appearing and disappearing is one number in one plan, and the plan is the only place the breakpoint is written down. Slack and alignment. When a row's children keep natural widths, the run may not fill the view — and where the run sits is said with structure, not a knob: a Spacer [ ] child absorbs the slack. Between two groups it pushes them apart; one on each side centers the run; one first right-aligns it. Shares are cut from what the naturals leave, so shares adding to 100 leave no slack at all and a Spacer beside them collapses — shares fill; naturals align. Across the flow, the layout places every child — y in a row, x in a stack, in every plan. Where each one sits there is the layout's align: start unless it says otherwise, and a plan entry may say otherwise for its own tier. A plan entry's offset shifts one named child from where align put it — a nudge that belongs to that arrangement, so it goes away with the tier, which is exactly when it stops meaning anything: actions: View [ width = 100%, layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [ { from: 420, flow: "row", gap: 18, align: "center", offset: { source: 1 } }, { from: 0, flow: "stack", gap: 14 }, ] } ], run: Button [ width = 240, height = 46 ], // the row centres the pair on it source: Text [ text = "View & edit source →" ], ] So a child under a ResponsiveLayout declares neither x nor y — the checker says so at the line, and says which of these to use instead. A child that needs a finer arrangement of its own contents is the next case down: give it a layout of its own. Nesting — who decides what. A ResponsiveLayout watches its own view's width — not the window's. The parent's plan decides how much room each child gets; each child decides what to do with the room it got — if the child has its own ResponsiveLayout, its plans answer to its own width, automatically. Room flows down; each level responds locally. (A plan can only name direct children — managing a grandchild is the child's own plan's business.) This is the answer to most things a plan cannot say by itself, and it wants no class: an ordinary inline child carries its own layout: like any other view. A component nested this way answers to its allocation, not the window — the same child reads correctly in a sidebar, a dialog, or a full-bleed row, and picks its own flow in each. One thing to get right: the parent's plan must actually give the child a width in every tier. A tier that allocates it nothing leaves it at its content width, and a child sized by its content is measuring what it is trying to arrange — so name it in the stack tier's shares (share: { acts: 100 }) or give it width = 100%. Division of labor. ResponsiveLayout manages named regions. A collection of uniform, replicated cards that should reflow to fit is the other tool: WrappingLayout (it wraps by fitting, no plan needed) with a width constraint on the card. Padding, and what from then means. The inset is the view's (View.padding), and a plan is selected against the content width, with the shares dividing it — so a padded bar's tiers answer to the room its children actually get, and from: 600 means 600 of usable room, not 600 of outer width. When the rules aren't enough. A plan speaks width, flow, share, and gap. Reach for nesting first, and most of the time last: give the part that needs its own mind a layout: of its own and let it arrange itself inside the room this plan hands it (above). A child that decides for itself is almost always the answer to "this plan cannot say what I need", and it composes — the same child then reads correctly wherever it is put. Past that: whole alternate configurations beyond geometry are a State applied on a width condition; fully custom geometry is a subclass overriding place() — the same seam every layout in the library is built on.

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout.plan
entries.text: The storyboard: a list of { from, flow, share?, gap?, align?, offset? } entries. from means "use this plan when the view is at least this wide" — the largest from that fits wins, wherever it sits in the list, and from: 0 is the fallback. flow is "row" or "stack". share divides width in either flow — not row-only: a "stack" entry may carry shares, and they set each band's width. It names the children by their own child names , checked when the layout first arranges — a name with no child is a loud error. A share of 0 drops that child while the plan is active — out of the flow, its space reclaimed — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is one number rather than a narrow ? … : … branch, and they return by themselves when the view widens. A child a plan does not name keeps its natural width, and a row's shares divide what is left after it — the gaps and the naturals both come out before the percentages are cut, so 60 means 60% of the remainder and a fixed-width logo composes beside two proportional regions with no arithmetic by hand. "auto" is the word for that said out loud (share: { logo: "auto", nav: 60, actions: 40 }): identical geometry to leaving the child out, and the opposite of 0 — 0 drops the child, "auto" keeps it at the size it chose for itself. In a stack "auto" is accepted and changes nothing, since a stack's shares are widths and its flow axis is height. align and offset are per tier. A plan entry's align — a string, "start", "center", "end" or "baseline" — overrides the layout's own for that tier, as its gap does. Its offset names children the way share does and shifts each one across the flow — down in a row, right in a stack — by a signed number of pixels from where align placed it. A name with no child, or an offset that is not a number, is an error naming it. Two values are refused where the plan is read. A row whose shares add to more than 100 is an error naming the plan and the total — a row's shares divide one run and cannot claim more of it than there is. (A stack's do not compete: each is an independent percent of the view, so { logo: 100, nav: 100 } is the full-bleed idiom, not an overflow — but a single share above 100 is refused in either flow.) And a share that is neither a number from 0 to 100 nor "auto" is an error naming the child, instead of a NaN width. array

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout.gap
entries.text: The default space between children, overridable per plan entry. number

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout.align
entries.text: Where children sit across the flow — y in a row, x in a stack: start (the default), center, end, or baseline. A bare literal here; a plan entry overrides it with a string (align: "center"). center and end work in the band: the view's own cross content extent, or the tallest (widest) laid child on a view that sizes itself from these very children — the same band as SimpleLayout's align. baseline sits every child of a row on one text line, each child declaring its own (a Text does; a composite says which part carries it), and is refused on a stack tier, which has no line. There is no none: this layout places the cross axis in every tier, so it always says where. CrossAlign

entries.title: ResponsiveLayout.place
entries.text: Selects the active plan from the view's own width — never the window's — and arranges accordingly: both axes of every child, along the flow by the plan and across it by align and offset. That is what makes nesting work: the parent's plan decides how much room a child gets, and the child's own plan answers to the room it got, automatically. A plan can only name direct children; managing a grandchild is the child's plan's business. place()

entries.title: Spacer
entries.text: When a row (or stack) does not fill its container, the leftover space has to go somewhere — and the laid children cannot take it themselves (their flow-axis slot is owned by the layout). A Spacer says where, structurally: put one between two groups and they push apart ("logo left, actions right"); put one on each side of a run and it centers; put one first and the run right-aligns. Several spacers split the slack evenly. When there is no slack — a plan whose shares fill the width, an auto-sized container — a Spacer is simply zero and invisible in effect. The layout owns a Spacer's flow-axis size (a percent-family constraint, so a container deriving its extent from its children never counts one); the flexes marker is what a flow layout looks for. An empty view otherwise — it paints nothing and has no size of its own.

entries.title: Spacer.flexes
entries.text: The marker a flow layout looks for. True (the default) means the layout owns this Spacer's size along the flow axis and expands it to take up the slack — which is what makes Spacer [ ] push its siblings apart. Set it false for a fixed gap you size yourself. boolean

entries.title: Spacer.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Spacer.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Table
entries.text: The list collection, componentized: the selection-bearing, scroll-owning frame around a replicated (or written) collection, carrying the selection model so no app hand-rolls it again: Selection is the Table's value — selected (the primary member) and selection (all of them, presented order), holding members: the record for a replicated row, the row view itself for a written one. App-ownable via input; identity by the usual ladder (a record's id by convention, else the object itself — the reconciler's own rule). The three facts: selection, the anchor (where ranges extend from), and the keyboard position active — moved by arrows, extended by shift, walked alone by ⌘ with Space toggling (discontiguous keyboard selection). selects declares the mode: none single multi (default single). Rows are TableRow instances — the RadioGroup discipline: direct children reaching their table as parent, replicated over data or written by hand. The row template stays free of any selection wiring. Windowing composes: put virtualize on the row template and selection, ranges, and keyboard travel keep working — members are read from the data through any row's cursor, never from instances, so an unmaterialized row can be range-selected and arrow travel scrolls it into existence (rows are assumed uniform in height). Table [ width = 300, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value }, selects = "multi", input(sel: object) { app.chosen = sel }, TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 30, t: TextLabel [ x = 8, text = :label ] ] ] App [ width = 320, height = 200, d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "label": "Ada" }, { "id": 2, "label": "Grace" }, { "id": 3, "label": "Alan" } ] } }, t: Table [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 100, datapath = { d.value }, selects = "multi", TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 26, Text [ x = 8, y = center, text = :label ] ] ], Text [ x = 20, y = 140, text = { (t.selection ?? []).length + " selected" } ] ]

entries.title: Table.selected
entries.text: The primary selected member — the record most recently selected, or null. Members, not views: selection survives sorts, filters, and windowing because it was never a set of instances. object

entries.title: Table.selection
entries.text: Every selected member, in presented order — null when nothing is selected. Records for a replicated table, the row views themselves for a written one. Never assign it; deliver through input. array

entries.title: Table.active
entries.text: The member the keyboard stands on — moved by arrows, and distinct from the selection, which is what makes ⌘-walk-then-Space possible. object

entries.title: Table.selects
entries.text: The mode: "none", "single" (the default), or "multi". Multi is what enables shift-ranges, ⌘-toggles, and the ⌘-walk. string

entries.title: Table.scrolls
entries.text: none | y | x | both

entries.title: Table.clip
entries.text: Shape

entries.title: Table.idOf
entries.text: A member's identity: its scalar id field by convention, else the object itself — the same ladder the reconciler uses, so nothing needs declaring for selection to survive a re-sort . idOf(m)

entries.title: Table.same
entries.text: Whether two members are the same one, by idOf. same(a, b)

entries.title: Table.isSelected
entries.text: Whether a member is in the selection, by identity. isSelected(m)

entries.title: Table.isActive
entries.text: Whether a member is the keyboard position, by identity. isActive(m)

entries.title: Table.input
entries.text: Where the selection goes. The default writes selected and selection; override it to own the value (input(sel: object) { app.chosen = sel }) and every gesture — click, range, keyboard — routes through your override, because they all land here. input(sel)

entries.title: Table.clearSelection
entries.text: Delivers an empty selection through input. clearSelection()

entries.title: Table.memberAt
entries.text: The member at a logical index. memberAt(i)

entries.title: Table.memberArray
entries.text: The full member universe, read from the data through any row's cursor — never from instances. This is the windowing contract: a table over a virtualized collection can range-select rows that have never been built. memberArray()

entries.title: Table.memberCount
entries.text: How many members there are — the full logical count, not what is materialized. memberCount()

entries.title: Table.rowClick
entries.text: The click protocol: plain click selects exactly one member, ⌘/Ctrl toggles, Shift extends from the anchor. Called by a TableRow; override to change what a click means. rowClick(i, m, toggle, range)

entries.title: Table.step
entries.text: Arrow-key travel: plain moves and selects, Shift extends the range, ⌘ moves the position alone so Space can toggle it. Scrolls the destination into view. step(to, e)

entries.title: Table.showRow
entries.text: Scrolls a row into view by index — using its instance when one exists, and arithmetic when it does not , so arrow travel into unmaterialized rows works and materializes on arrival. showRow(i)

entries.title: Table.deleteRequested
entries.text: Delivery seam — the app declares what deleting is. Fires on Delete or Backspace while there is a selection and the table itself holds focus, so a text field's Backspace is never mistaken for it. Does nothing by default: refusal by inertness. deleteRequested()

entries.title: Table.activateRequested
entries.text: Delivery seam — the app declares what opening is. Fires on Enter on the walked row, under the same focus condition. The list idiom's other half. activateRequested()

entries.title: Table.keyDown
entries.text: Arrows, Home/End, Space (multi), Delete/Backspace and Enter. An override should call through or the table loses its keyboard. onKeyDown(e)

entries.title: TableRow
entries.text: One row of a Table: a direct child of it, replicated over data (datapath = :rows[]) or written by hand. A row carries no selection wiring of its own — it reads whether it is selected or active from its table, and hands clicks to the table's rowClick. It is never a tab stop: the table holds focus, so the arrow keys land on the container. App [ width = 320, height = 170, d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "label": "Ada" }, { "id": 2, "label": "Grace" } ] } }, t: Table [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 220, height = 60, datapath = { d.value }, TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 28, Text [ x = 8, y = center, text = { :label + (parent.selected ? " ✓" : "") } ] ] ], Text [ x = 20, y = 110, text = "Click a row: its own selected fact follows." ] ]

entries.title: TableRow.selected
entries.text: Whether this row's member is in its table's selection — derived from the table, never stored. boolean

entries.title: TableRow.active
entries.text: Whether this row is its table's keyboard position. boolean

entries.title: TableRow.focusable
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: TableRow.width
entries.text: As wide as its table; a row never sizes itself. Length

entries.title: TableRow.fill
entries.text: Selected takes the selected tint, hovered the hover tint, otherwise none — a row is transparent so the table's own ground shows through. Fill

entries.title: TableRow.stroke
entries.text: The active row shows an accent ring only while the table's focus is visible (keyboard, not pointer) — the rule every control's focus ring follows. Stroke

entries.title: TableRow.member
entries.text: The member this row presents: its record when replicated, the row view itself when written by hand. member()

entries.title: TableRow.rowIndex
entries.text: This row's logical index in data order — read from the cursor when replicated, so it is true under windowing. A method rather than a slot because its consumers are gestures, and the written-row fallback walks children, which no constraint may do. rowIndex()

entries.title: TableRow.pointerDown
entries.text: Focuses the table, not the row — rows are never tab stops, so the arrow keys must land on the container. onPointerDown()

entries.title: TableRow.click
entries.text: Delivers the click to the table's rowClick with the modifier state. Override rowClick on the table rather than this, unless a particular row needs to opt out. onClick()

entries.title: Combobox
entries.text: Filter-as-you-type over a collection: a text field owning a query plus a dismissable option list owning a choice — a derived selection over data. Composition, not invention: TextInput for the entry, the Menu machinery for the list (overlay, raise, light-dismiss, Escape closes — the whole dismissal discipline rides along), and the matches are a derived collection — a constraint over the items array, so the live match count is free and no rendered row is ever scanned. Combobox [ width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee", items = { app.people }, input(v: object) { app.assignee = v } ] Items are members (the selection model's currency): records — shown by their label (or id) — or plain strings. value holds the chosen member; input(v) is the delivery seam: the default writes value, a use-site override redirects and the slot stays untouched. Typing filters live (case-insensitive substring); opening without typing shows the full list (the disclosure-button path). Picking echoes the label into the field and closes; editing again re-filters from the new text. Keyboard: arrows rove the list (the Menu rover), Enter picks the roved row — or the first match when none is roved (the type-then-Enter path); Escape closes the list (then a second Escape leaves the control — the focus-scope ascent). The list is never a tab stop of its own. The list is a collection like any other — bind 100k options and virtualize applies to it the same way (via the Menu it composes). App [ width = 320, height = 160, picked: string = "", people: array = { ["Ada Lovelace", "Grace Hopper", "Alan Turing", "Barbara Liskov"] }, Combobox [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee", items = { app.people }, input(v: object) { app.picked = "" + v } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.picked == "" ? "—" : app.picked } ] ]

entries.title: Combobox.items
entries.text: The options, as members: records — shown by their label, else id — or plain strings. The currency of the selection model, so whatever you put in is what comes back out of input. array

entries.title: Combobox.value
entries.text: The chosen member, not the typed text — the whole record when you supplied records. null until something is picked. Standalone the combobox owns it; constrained, override input beside it. object

entries.title: Combobox.placeholder
entries.text: The entry's placeholder text while empty. string

entries.title: Combobox.query
entries.text: What the user has typed since the last pick. Not the value — the draft that filters the list. string

entries.title: Combobox.filtering
entries.text: Whether the user has typed since the last pick. False means a bare disclosure, which shows the whole list rather than filtering against a stale query — the difference between clicking the chevron and typing. boolean

entries.title: Combobox.matches
entries.text: The filtered options, as a derived collection: a constraint over items, so the live match count is free and no rendered row is ever scanned. Case-insensitive substring against each member's label. array

entries.title: Combobox.matchCount
entries.text: How many options currently match — read it straight, rather than counting list rows, which is both wrong under virtualization and refused by the compiler. number

entries.title: Combobox.list
entries.text: The option list — a Menu created at the app layer on first open, not a child of the combobox, so it paints over everything rather than only over later siblings. All the overlay behaviour arrives with it: light dismiss, Escape, the arrow rover, the viewport flip, the long-list scroll. View

entries.title: Combobox.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Combobox.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Combobox.labelOf
entries.text: How a member is displayed: a record's label, else its id, else the value itself. Override to display members your own way. labelOf(m)

entries.title: Combobox.input
entries.text: Where the choice goes. Receives the chosen member. The default writes value; an override redirects it and leaves the slot untouched. input(v)

entries.title: Combobox.pickIndex
entries.text: Picks the nth current match: echoes its label into the entry, closes the list, and delivers the member through input. The index is into matches, never into items. pickIndex(i)

entries.title: Combobox.ensureList
entries.text: Creates the shared list on first use and wires its delivery back to pickIndex. ensureList()

entries.title: Combobox.syncList
entries.text: Pushes the current matches into the list — called on every keystroke. syncList()

entries.title: Combobox.closeList
entries.text: Closes the list without picking. closeList()

entries.title: Combobox.listShown
entries.text: Whether the list is currently up. listShown()

entries.title: Combobox.listRoved
entries.text: Whether the keyboard rover is sitting on a row. This is what makes Enter mean two things : pick the roved row when there is one, else take the first match — the type-then-Enter path. listRoved()

entries.title: Combobox.open
entries.text: Opens the full list unfiltered — the disclosure-button path. open()

entries.title: Combobox.toggle
entries.text: Opens the list, or closes it if it is already open. toggle()

entries.title: ContextMenu
entries.text: The right-click / long-press menu: Menu's machinery whole — overlay, raise, pointer-anchored placement with viewport clamping, the Mac light-dismiss rule (an outside press closes and is swallowed), Escape closes the chain — with a gesture-opened entry. It has no overlay machinery of its own; whatever it does, Menu does. Declared once, opened by many. The serving view declares the gesture — that declaration is what routes it (the claim model: contextMenu engages the right-click/two-finger path, hold is the touch long-press gate, and each engages only where a handler is declared). The whole wiring is two lines on the view the menu serves: rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { … }, picked(id: string) { … } ], … Row [ …, onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) }, onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) } ] open(v, e) anchors at the pointer (view-relative event coordinates walked to root space) and clamps inside the app — Menu's own placement discipline. Items are the standard Menu records — written lists or derived from the opener (items = { … opener … } for per-row menus with zero per-row instances); picking delivers through picked(id) and closes. Everything else — items, opener, picked, the rover, the cascade, dismissal — is Menu's, documented there. App [ width = 320, height = 130, chose: string = "", rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { [ ({ id: "open", label: "Open" }), ({ id: "rename", label: "Rename" }), ({ divider: true }), ({ id: "delete", label: "Delete" }) ] }, picked(id: string) { app.chose = id } ], card: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 44, cornerRadius = 8, fill = darkslategray, onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) }, onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) }, Text [ x = 12, y = center, text = "Right-click or hold me" ] ], Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.chose == "" ? "—" : app.chose } ] ]

entries.title: ContextMenu.open
entries.text: Opens the menu anchored at the pointer, given the serving view and the pointer event — Menu.openAt under the name the two-line wiring reads best with. The serving view declares the gesture, and that declaration is what routes it : onContextMenu engages the right-click and two-finger path, onHold the touch long-press. Neither engages anywhere a handler is not declared, so a context menu costs nothing on views that do not offer one. open(v, e)

entries.title: DataGrid
entries.text: The Table contract plus a column model: headers, sortable, reorderable and resizable by drag, touch-correct, over a windowed collection. DataGrid [ width = 600, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value }, selects = "multi", Column [ title = "ID", field = "id", width = 70 ], Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 280 ], Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ], GridRow [ datapath = :rows[], virtualize = true ] ] Columns are written members (Column: permanent, authored, its identity the child itself): title heads the column, field names what a cell shows, width is the authored width — a plain value (the column model follows which columns exist, not a column's own attributes; a responsive width belongs in the grid's widths state, which is a tracked dependency: widths = { app.narrow ? ({ id: 40, … }) : null }). A column's id is its field (title as fallback). Order and widths are the grid's value-pattern state: order (column ids, presented order) and widths (id → width overrides). Reorder delivers through arrangeInput(order), resize through resizeInput(id, w) — the defaults write the slots; an app override owns them (persisted layouts). Widths are plain values — nothing measures cells. Header interactions: click sorts — a delivery (sortInput(on, dir), writing sortOn/sortDir by default): sort names a derivation, the truth stays in data (the app derives the sorted dataset; a grid displays the order its collection has). Horizontal drag reorders (the new order commits on release); the right-edge grip resizes. Both drags declare claim = x — on touch the page keeps vertical pan while the drag owns x. Rows: the use site writes one bare GridRow template over its rows path — cells generate from the column model, each showing record[field]. Selection, keyboard, windowing: Table's, unchanged — virtualize on the template windows the grid, and the header (a preceding sibling) offsets the window's geometry. Focus: the grid lands as one tab stop, in browse mode — arrows navigate rows. Narrow widths: a cell clips; a widths entry of 0 drops its column entirely — priority, not squish. Selection, keyboard travel and windowing are Table's, documented there. What follows is only the column model. App [ width = 440, height = 220, d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "title": "Fix the rail", "state": "open" }, { "id": 2, "title": "Draft the chapter", "state": "done" }, { "id": 3, "title": "Measure the grid", "state": "open" } ] } }, DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 50, width = 400, height = 130, datapath = { d.value }, selects = "multi", Column [ title = "ID", field = "id", width = 50 ], Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 220 ], Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ], GridRow [ datapath = :rows[] ] ] ] Drag a header sideways to reorder; drag the divider between two headers to resize; click a header to sort.

entries.title: DataGrid.headerH
entries.text: The header row's height. number

entries.title: DataGrid.order
entries.text: The presented column order, as column ids — null means authored order. Part of the grid's value-pattern state: delivered through arrangeInput, so an app that overrides that owns the order and can persist it. array

entries.title: DataGrid.widths
entries.text: Per-column width overrides, { id: width } — null means authored widths. A width of 0 drops the column entirely , which is the deliberate narrow-screen degrade: priority, not squish. widths = { app.narrow ? ({ notes: 0 }) : null } is a responsive layout. object

entries.title: DataGrid.sortOn
entries.text: The column id the sort names — "" when unsorted. Sorting names a derivation; it does not reorder anything. The truth stays in the data: your app derives the sorted dataset from this, and the grid displays the order its collection already has. string

entries.title: DataGrid.sortDir
entries.text: "asc" or "desc", alongside sortOn. string

entries.title: DataGrid.escaped
entries.text: Whether the header surface has left the grid's scrolling box for its parent. The grid's box is the rows' scroll region exactly — the scrollbar spans rows only, and no row ever slides under the header. Backends without the ride keep an in-box header. How it settles The request is made at init and applied by the runtime at attach; one deferred read records the answer. A false that survives means the backend has no ride at all. boolean

entries.title: DataGrid.sortInput
entries.text: Delivery seam for sorting. The default writes sortOn/sortDir; override it to own the sort — which is what you do when the sorted collection is derived app-side, or when the sort belongs to a server query. sortInput(on, dir)

entries.title: DataGrid.arrangeInput
entries.text: Delivery seam for reordering, receiving the new column-id order. Override it to persist a user's column layout. arrangeInput(ord)

entries.title: DataGrid.resizeInput
entries.text: Delivery seam for resizing, receiving a column id and its new width. Widths are plain values — nothing measures cells — so an override is free to clamp, snap, or store them. resizeInput(id, w)

entries.title: DataGrid.headerClick
entries.text: Toggles the sort on a column: same column flips direction, a new column starts ascending. Routes through sortInput. headerClick(id)

entries.title: DataGrid.columnRecords
entries.text: The derived column model — the authored Column children, ordered and widthed by state, with running x offsets. The one truth every header cell and grid cell positions from. Its inputs arrive as arguments — the grid's childViews, order and widths — so the model re-derives when a column is added or removed, or the order or widths change. columnRecords(kids, ord, w)

entries.title: DataGrid.colId
entries.text: A column's id: its field, falling back to its title. colId(c)

entries.title: DataGrid.currentOrder
entries.text: The column ids in their present order. currentOrder()

entries.title: DataGrid.editStep
entries.text: Moves an active "edit" cell's focus one row up or down in the same column — the spreadsheet expectation. Scrolls the destination into existence first, so it works over a windowed collection. editStep(row, field, d)

entries.title: DataGrid.colWidthOf
entries.text: The present width of a column by id. colWidthOf(id)

entries.title: DataGrid.openSelect
entries.text: Opens the shared options menu for a "select" cell and writes the picked value into the record through the row's cursor. One menu serves every select cell in the grid. openSelect(row, cell, field, current)

entries.title: DataGrid.init
entries.text: Requests the header's escape from the scroll box (see escaped). The request stands: the runtime applies it when the view attaches, so init running before attach costs nothing. onInit()

entries.title: Column
entries.text: One column of a DataGrid: a written member, never replicated — permanent, authored, its identity the child itself. title heads it, field names what each cell shows, kind says what a cell is, and width is its authored width. A column's id is its field, with title as the fallback. A column draws nothing itself (visible is false): the grid builds headers and cells from the column model. App [ width = 400, height = 170, d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "task": "Write", "done": true }, { "id": 2, "task": "Ship", "done": false } ] } }, DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 340, height = 110, datapath = { d.value }, Column [ title = "Task", field = "task", kind = "edit", width = 220 ], Column [ title = "Done", field = "done", kind = "check", width = 80 ], GridRow [ datapath = :rows[] ] ] ]

entries.title: Column.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record a Column styles its cells off — a provided value the app provides once (App [ theme = { … } ]) and the grid reads. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: Column.title
entries.text: The column's heading text. Also its identity when field is empty. string

entries.title: Column.field
entries.text: The record key this column shows, and the column's id. A cell renders record[field] — there is no per-cell template to write. string

entries.title: Column.kind
entries.text: What a cell is: "text" (the default, a static label), "edit" (a TextInput committing every keystroke into the record), "check" (a Checkbox over a boolean field), or "select" (the value plus a chevron, opening the shared options menu). string

entries.title: Column.options
entries.text: The choices a "select" cell offers — records or strings. Read at gesture time, not baked into the column model , so it may be a constraint that changes with app state. array

entries.title: Column.visible
entries.text: boolean

entries.title: Column.width
entries.text: Length

entries.title: GridRow
entries.text: The row template of a DataGrid: write one bare GridRow over the rows path (GridRow [ datapath = :rows[] ]) and its cells generate from the column model, each showing record[field]. Selection, keyboard travel and windowing are TableRow's and Table's, unchanged; virtualize = true on the template windows the grid. App [ width = 400, height = 200, d: Dataset [ contents = { { rows: [...Array(500).keys()].map((i) => ({ id: i, n: "row " + i })) } } ], DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 300, height = 150, datapath = { d.value }, Column [ title = "Name", field = "n", width = 280 ], GridRow [ datapath = :rows[], virtualize = true ] ] ]

entries.title: GridRow.rec
entries.text: The row's record, as a derived slot. A slot rather than a method call, so cells re-derive when the record's fields change — a method read would go stale. null on a written (unreplicated) row. object

entries.title: GridRow.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: GridRow.setText
entries.text: Writes a text value into the field a column names, in this row's record — :@[(field)] = v. A cell calls it rather than writing itself, because a cell's own cursor is its column, not the row. setText(field, v)

entries.title: GridRow.setFlag
entries.text: The same for a boolean field — what a "check" cell calls. setFlag(field, v)

entries.title: Segmented
entries.text: A row of mutually exclusive choices — the control you reach for when the options are few, named, and worth showing all at once. Its choices are data, like Menu's items and DataGrid's columns: Segmented [ width = 300, value = { app.page }, choices = { [ ({ id: "controls", label: "Controls" }), ({ id: "table", label: "Table" }), ({ id: "grid", label: "DataGrid" }) ] }, input(v: string) { app.page = v } ] Why data, and not Segment children Because the sliding highlight cannot be built any other way. The pill has to know which choice is selected and how wide each one is, and a constraint may not ask the view tree that: childViews carries set membership only, so .length is live while anything reaching into the collection is refused — aggregation over a reactive node collection … derive from data [DECLARE7001]. The compiler names the answer. Equal widths Segments divide the control's width evenly — a segmented control divides evenly, where a row of buttons sizes to its content. Equal width keeps the convention that segment labels are short and similar in length, and it lets the pill travel at constant width between segments. So a Segmented does not size itself to its labels : set width, or accept segMin × choices.length. The pill The highlight springs a normalized lane — a float index — not pixels. x is then lane × segW, so a resize recomputes segW and the pill snaps to the right place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. The chosen segment wears a raised surface pill with a hairline. App [ width = 340, height = 130, page: string = "one", Segmented [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 300, value = { app.page }, choices = { [ ({ id: "one", label: "One" }), ({ id: "two", label: "Two" }), ({ id: "three", label: "Three" }) ] }, input(v: string) { app.page = v } ], Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { "showing: " + app.page } ] ]

entries.title: Segmented.theme
entries.text: The provided design-token record this widget styles off — a provided value (the app provides it once with App [ theme = { … } ]; Control and the library widgets read it). Reads theme.accent and its kin as typed members; defaults to the house look. See Control.theme. Theme

entries.title: Segmented.choices
entries.text: The segments, as records: { id, label } or { id, icon } — the same vocabulary Menu's items use. A choice shows a label or an icon, never both. A choice may also carry a location, which makes that segment a real link (see SegmentedItem.location). array

entries.title: Segmented.value
entries.text: The active choice. Constrain it to your own state and override input to own the destination, or leave it alone and read value back — a Segmented works standalone. Compared against each choice's id by identity, so any value type works. object

entries.title: Segmented.disabled
entries.text: Disables the whole control. A segment is not separately disable-able — a disabled group leaves the tab order entirely rather than offering unreachable stops. boolean

entries.title: Segmented.segMin
entries.text: The per-segment width used when you set no width on the control. Because a Segmented does not self-size to its labels, this is what decides the default width: segMin × choices.length. number

entries.title: Segmented.count
entries.text: How many choices there are, floored at 1 so the width arithmetic never divides by zero. number

entries.title: Segmented.segW
entries.text: One segment's width — the control's width divided by the count. What the pill and every segment position from. number

entries.title: Segmented.idx
entries.text: Which choice is live, as an index into choices, from the data — the only place the question can be asked. −1 (nothing selected) parks the pill at 0 and hides it rather than springing to a phantom slot. number

entries.title: Segmented.lane
entries.text: The pill's position as a float index, sprung toward idx. The whole reason the pill is correct at any size: x is lane × segW, so a resize recomputes the width and the pill snaps to the right place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. number

entries.title: Segmented.height
entries.text: Length

entries.title: Segmented.cornerRadius
entries.text: Radius

entries.title: Segmented.fill
entries.text: The quiet control tint for the track; the picked segment paints its own. Fill

entries.title: Segmented.opacity
entries.text: Disabled dims the whole control — track, pill and every segment alike, never a recolour — to the theme's disabledOpacity, or 0.45 when the theme states none. number

entries.title: Segmented.width
entries.text: Content-sized: every segment at least segMin wide, so short labels never squeeze. Length

entries.title: Segmented.datapath
entries.text: Roots the control on its own items data, so the segments replicate from choices without the author writing a datapath. datapath

entries.title: Segmented.input
entries.text: Where the choice goes, receiving the picked id. The default writes value; override it to own the destination. input(v)

entries.title: Segmented.pick
entries.text: Selects a choice by id, routing through input. The seam a segment calls. pick(v)

entries.title: Segmented.segs
entries.text: The segment views, for the keyboard rove. A handler-only walk — a constraint may not aggregate the view tree. segs()

entries.title: Segmented.roveFrom
entries.text: Moves keyboard focus to the adjacent segment. Arrows rove; Space or Enter picks where they land, so an inactive choice is reachable and selectable entirely from the keyboard . roveFrom(seg, d)

entries.title: ChevronIcon
entries.text: The disclosure mark: a menu drops, a pane opens, a select expands. Every disclosure in the chrome is this one class turned by its dir, which is what makes them agree. For a direction that is itself the state — a sort order, a trend — reach for ArrowIcon instead; the two must not look alike.

entries.title: ChevronIcon.dir
entries.text: The resting orientation: "down" (the default), "up", "left" or "right". Sugar over angle. string

entries.title: ChevronIcon.angle
entries.text: The rotation in radians, and the primitive, so it can be sprung — an Accordion twisty turns in step with its pane sliding open rather than snapping between two states. The turn lives in the recording deliberately: the mark rotates inside its 16-box while the box stays put. (The View-level rotation attribute turns the whole box — the wrong tool for a glyph whose frame should not move.) number

entries.title: ChevronIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the chevron. Override to replace the mark while keeping the class's role. draw(d)

entries.title: CheckIcon
entries.text: The tick — a checked menu row, a Checkbox's mark, a confirmation. Ink stays local : a menu row inverts its check on the highlighted row while a checkbox always uses the accent text color, so the host sets ink rather than the icon assuming it.

entries.title: CheckIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the tick. One shape, one stroke, one join — so a checkbox's mark and a menu row's check cannot drift apart. draw(d)

entries.title: CloseIcon
entries.text: The dismiss mark: a window close box, a chip's remove affordance, a dialog's corner.

entries.title: CloseIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the cross. draw(d)

entries.title: PlusIcon
entries.text: Add. Pairs with MinusIcon at the same stroke and cap, so a stepper's two ends match.

entries.title: PlusIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the plus. draw(d)

entries.title: MinusIcon
entries.text: Remove, and the partially-checked state of a tri-state box. Pairs with PlusIcon.

entries.title: MinusIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the bar. draw(d)

entries.title: LightbulbIcon
entries.text: The help affordance — the one FILLED mark in a stroked set: a continuous teardrop of glass over a three-bar tapering base.

entries.title: LightbulbIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the bulb. This one mark is filled, and does not answer to weight — the contour carries its weight in the outline itself, so there is no stroke to widen. The bulb keeps its own visual weight at every rung. draw(d)

entries.title: SunIcon
entries.text: "Light" in the appearance triad — a disc with rays, sharing its radius and stroke with MoonIcon and AutoIcon so the three read as one family at 14px.

entries.title: SunIcon.rays
entries.text: How many rays surround the disc. Eight by default; lowering it reads lighter at small sizes. number

entries.title: SunIcon.solid
entries.text: false (the default) draws the ring; true fills the disc. The ring is drawn a touch smaller than the filled disc on purpose — a stroke straddles its path, so an outline at the filled radius reads as the larger mark. boolean

entries.title: SunIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the disc and its rays. draw(d)

entries.title: MoonIcon
entries.text: "Dark" in the appearance triad. The crescent is the region between two equal circles , the second offset by (3, −3) — so both arcs meet exactly at the circles' intersection points and the horns close to a point instead of leaving the ragged tail an arc pair leaves.

entries.title: MoonIcon.solid
entries.text: false (the default) strokes the closed path — the tapered-horn rendition; true fills it for a solid crescent. One path, two renditions — nothing about the geometry changes, only what is done with it. boolean

entries.title: MoonIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the crescent. draw(d)

entries.title: AutoIcon
entries.text: "System" in the appearance triad — the same disc, half of it taken away. The ring stays around the empty half so it reads as part of one object rather than as a gap. The one mark of the three whose meaning is its fill, which is why a mixed outline-and-filled language is right for the triad.

entries.title: AutoIcon.draw
entries.text: Renders the half-filled disc. draw(d)

entries.title: Icon
entries.text: A small monochrome mark, drawn rather than typed. A font's glyphs are not marks: they are not guaranteed to be present, they rasterize differently on every platform, and the ones that exist are the wrong shapes — a ✓ sits on the text baseline and reads like a square-root sign, not like a checkmark. The library's own marks — Checkbox.mark, Menu.check, the Combobox disclosure — are all Icons. Writing one Subclass and override draw. Author the shape in a 16×16 box — unit converts it to whatever size the host asked for: class SparkIcon extends Icon [ draw(d: Draw) { d.scale(unit, unit) d.strokeStyle = ink; d.lineWidth = weight / unit d.beginPath(); d.moveTo(8, 1); d.lineTo(8, 15); d.stroke() } ] Overriding a method is how a subclass refines an icon — a subclass cannot re-declare a child it inherits (the compiler refuses it) — so the shape lives in draw and everything adjustable is a slot. Size changes the drawing, not the shape Every icon is one path. There are no per-size variants, no thresholds, nothing redrawn at a breakpoint: unit scales the 16-box to whatever the host asked for, so a 64px icon is the 16px icon at 4×, exactly. The stroke is the deliberate exception. d.lineWidth = weight / unit sits inside d.scale(unit, unit), so the two cancel and the line lands at a constant weight in device pixels at every size. An icon's line therefore matches the 1px rules and text weights it sits among, instead of fattening as it grows. The cost is that the stroke-to-size ratio falls: 1.6px is 10% of a 16px icon, 5% at 32, 2.5% at 64. Across 14–18px — chrome sizes — that is invisible. Past ~32 an icon starts reading as a fine-line drawing rather than a mark — so this set is built for chrome sizes , and a large display icon (an empty-state mark, an about-box graphic) would want the opposite: d.lineWidth = weight outside the scale, so the line grows with the drawing. What is not an Icon Application art. The desktop's dock icons are the case to look at before reaching for this class: they rest at 56px and grow under the magnification swell, they are polychrome (gradient(hue1, hue2) behind a hue-parameterised drawing), and their width animates every frame. Each of those alone rules them out — the constant stroke that suits a 16px mark is 2.9% of a 56px one and reads spindly; ink is a single colour; and an animated width is the one thing this set forbids. The line is not "drawn versus not drawn" — dock art is drawn too. It is chrome vocabulary versus identity. A mark that says close, expand, checked, this is the dark theme belongs here, at a size the host states. A mark that says this is Calendar does not, and belongs to the app that owns the identity. Desktop has both, which is what makes it the clarifying example: its menu rows take WindowIcon and CodeIcon from this set, while its dock keeps DockIcon. Two rules Scale inside the body, never with the View's scale. A recording rasterizes into a canvas sized to its own ink bounds at device resolution, while scale is a transform applied after — so scale = { width / 16 } would rasterize 16 pixels and stretch them. Crisp at exactly 16, soft at every other size, which is most of them. Scaling inside the recording allocates the raster at true size instead. Never animate an icon's width. Reading size inside draw makes the recording size-dependent: an animated size re-records and reallocates the backing canvas every frame, which drops a magnifying dock of icons from 60 to ~25fps. A static size re-records once and costs nothing after: 120 icons re-recording their content every frame run frame-bound at 16.6ms. Colour is not a rule — ink follows the provided text colour, so an icon beside a muted label goes muted on its own, and a host that needs a different ink (a menu row's check inverting on the hot row) simply sets it.

entries.title: Icon.iconSize
entries.text: The mark's size, in px — a provided value (a host states it once, every icon beneath answers): defaults to the nearest provided iconSize, overridable at the use site. number

entries.title: Icon.textColor
entries.text: The effective text colour the mark's ink follows — a provided value, so an icon beside a muted label goes muted on its own; set ink to override. Color

entries.title: Icon.ink
entries.text: The mark's colour. Follows the provided textColor, so an icon beside a muted label goes muted on its own. The trap: that slot falls back to black platform-wide, so an icon in a context that never states a text colour renders black and vanishes on a dark surface. State ink unless you know the context sets one — IconHost does it for every icon built by name. Color

entries.title: Icon.weight
entries.text: Stroke width in final device pixels, not authored ones. Divide by unit inside draw (d.lineWidth = weight / unit) and the scale cancels, so the line lands at a constant weight at every size and matches the 1px rules and text it sits among. number

entries.title: Icon.unit
entries.text: The 16-box-to-host-size scale factor. Multiply the path by it; divide the stroke by it. Every icon is one path at one size, scaled — there are no per-size variants. number

entries.title: Icon.width
entries.text: Sized by the provided iconSize, so a menu states 16 once and every icon in it answers; a use site may set its own. Length

entries.title: Icon.height
entries.text: Square, always — the height follows the width. Length

entries.title: Icon.y
entries.text: Length

entries.title: IconHost
entries.text: Turns an icon's class name into a live view. A control names its icon (iconLeft = "TrashIcon") rather than nesting one: a control is a leaf, and a name is the one form that is the same whether it is written or read from data. IconHost builds the named icon with createView, as a menu record's icon field does. It reserves no space when empty, so a control's contentWidth measures only the slots that are filled and an icon-less button needs no special case. The name is read once, when the host is built. A name read from data gives each row of a toolbar its own icon, but changing the name later does not swap the icon. An icon that must change at runtime — a play/pause toggle — is two icons, each with visible constrained.

entries.title: IconHost.kind
entries.text: The icon class name to build ("TrashIcon"). "" builds nothing and the host collapses to zero width, so an icon-less control needs no special case. Consumed once, at construction — assigning a new name later does not re-materialize the icon. A name that is only ever computed needs use [ Name ] to survive the build. string

entries.title: IconHost.iconSize
